Calendar.createEvent signature requires credentialId; other implementations still take one arg

The `Calendar` interface now declares `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number): Promise<NewCalendarEventType>`, but the other concrete implementations were not updated: `BaseCalendarService.createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts (line 125), `LarkCalendarService.createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` in packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts (line 125), and `Office365CalendarService.createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` in packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts (line 72) all declare `implements Calendar` and define `createEvent` with a single parameter. This is an interface/implementation mismatch that TypeScript will reject on build; every consumer of these apps (e.g., `createAllCalendarEvents` in EventManager) currently calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent)` without the new `credentialId`, so those code paths will not compile against the interface. Either make `credentialId` optional in the interface and update only Google, or update the three other services and all call sites to pass the credential id.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Only first destination calendar is persisted on the booking

The booking `data` block writes `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. The Booking schema has a single `destinationCalendar` relation, so only the first entry in `evt.destinationCalendar` is persisted. The PR’s stated goal is to invite every host to their own calendar, but on any later operation (reschedule, cancel, edit-location, request-reschedule) the booking record exposes only one destination. The other per-host calendar references survive only as BookingReference rows; deleting the booking.destinationCalendar connect for the event-type even on first creation breaks the previously persisted id reference for non-collective callers and silently drops the per-host mapping for re-runs. Either the schema needs to become a join table, or the booking should record which host’s calendar it was set under and consumers must be updated accordingly — this PR ships neither.

Team member shape adds unknown firstName/lastName empty fields

`teamMemberPromises` returns `firstName: "", lastName: ""` for every team member, but the `Person` type in `@calcom/types/Calendar` has no such keys (only `name`, `email`, `timeZone`, `language`, `username`, `id`, `bookingId`, `locale`, `timeFormat`, `bookingSeat`). Any strict object-literal usage would fail, and email/SMS renderers that iterate the object will get the empty strings. This was added without updating the type definition or any consumer — either the fields need to be added to `Person` and used by templates, or the spread of dead keys should be removed.

deleteEvent fallback also searches by externalId === externalCalendarId

Same defect as in `updateEvent`. `const calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — when `externalCalendarId` is null/empty the `find` predicate compares each calendar’s externalId against that same null/empty value, so the find never matches and the fallback always yields `undefined`. The eventual ternary `calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` then drops to `"primary"`, which is the wrong calendar for multi-host events and can delete from the wrong account or simply 404. Either use `event.destinationCalendar?.[0]?.externalId` for the fallback or restrict the lookup to a credentialId-keyed match.

evt.destinationCalendar?.push silently no-ops when null

Right above, `destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` is set. The follow-up `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }` uses optional chaining on a potentially null array — `null?.push` is just `undefined`, it does nothing and does not warn. For any COLLECTIVE event without an event-type or organizer destination calendar, no team members' destination calendars are attached to `evt`, even though they were collected into `teamDestinationCalendars`. Replace `?.push(...)` with an explicit `evt.destinationCalendar ??= []; evt.destinationCalendar.push(...)` (or build the final array once and assign it).

hosts.map users lack destinationCalendar, so teamDestinationCalendars stays empty

In the new loadUsers(), when the event has hosts, `users` is built via `hosts.map(({ user, isFixed }) => ({ ...user, isFixed }))`. The `user` record on each host is whatever Prisma returned for the relation; no explicit `select`/`include` is added, so relation fields like `destinationCalendar` are not present on those `user` objects. Downstream, `teamMemberPromises` does `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar)` and pushes to `teamDestinationCalendars` — this will always be undefined for host-loaded users, so `teamDestinationCalendars` ends up empty for COLLECTIVE team events. The whole point of this PR (multiple hosts receiving calendar events) silently fails whenever hosts come from the `eventType.hosts` relation.

loadUsers aggressively throws on empty dynamicUserList and is no longer required to return users

The new `loadUsers` wraps everything in try/catch and throws HttpError(500, "Unable to load users") for any non-HttpError/non-Prisma error, and adds new preconditions that the previous version lacked: `if (!Array.isArray(dynamicUserList) || dynamicUserList.length === 0) throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` and `if (!Array.isArray(hosts)) throw new Error("eventType.hosts is not properly defined.")`. Empty `dynamicUserList` was previously allowed to fall through to a normal empty result; a route that legitimately resolves no users (e.g., data issues) will now return 500/400 instead of being handled by upstream `ensureAvailableUsers` guards. Also, `return users.length ? users : eventType.users` evaluates eventType.users only after spreading hosts — for a non-host regular event this works, but for a team event with `eventType.schedulingType=ROUND_ROBIN` and no hosts it now returns the legacy `eventType.users` array and silently bypasses the host semantics the rest of the code expects.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token overwritten with literal string "refresh_token"

When `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is falsy, the code sets it to the literal string `"refresh_token"`. This is clearly placeholder/debug code that was never completed. When the sync endpoint returns a response that omits `refresh_token` (which is the expected case — the sync endpoint only returns access_token and expiry), the credential will be saved with `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`, permanently breaking token refresh for that user. Even in the non-sync path, any schema that doesn't require `refresh_token` (e.g., the Salesforce schema) will have its existing refresh_token overwritten by this literal string before the spread in the caller, unless the caller explicitly re-overwrites it (as Salesforce does, but Google Calendar and Office365 do not).

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Broken Zod schema for minimum token response

The `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` as computed property keys. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema returns a fixed string like `"ZodString"`, not a property name pattern. This does not create a schema that accepts any string key with a number value (as the comment suggests); instead it creates a single hardcoded key with an arbitrary name. When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, every call to `safeParse` will validate against this broken schema, likely rejecting all valid sync responses (or accepting them with wrong types). The intent was probably `z.record(z.string(), z.number()).optional()` or similar. All sync-path token refreshes will fail validation and throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned".

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync branch returns fetch Response, callers expect incompatible shapes

When the sync endpoint is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object. The callers expect completely different shapes: googlecalendar expects `{ res: { data: { access_token, expiry_date } } }` (from googleapis' `refreshToken`), hubspot expects a `HubspotToken` object (from `@hubspot/api-client`), zohocrm and zoho-bigin expect an axios response with `.data`. When sync is enabled, googlecalendar will do `res?.data` on a `Response` object (undefined), then `token.access_token` throws TypeError. Hubspot, zohocrm, and zoho-bigin will have similar shape mismatches. The function needs to normalize the sync endpoint response into the shape each caller expects.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

When the sync endpoint is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object. The callers expect completely different shapes: googlecalendar expects `{ res: { data: { access_token, expiry_date } } }` (from googleapis' `refreshToken`), hubspot expects a `HubspotToken` object (from `@hubspot/api-client`), zohocrm and zoho-bigin expect an axios response with `.data`. When sync is enabled, googlecalendar will do `res?.data` on a `Response` object (undefined), then `token.access_token` throws TypeError. Hubspot, zohocrm, and zoho-bigin will have similar shape mismatches. The function needs to normalize the sync endpoint response into the shape each caller expects.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unreliable response check and missing error handling

Two issues: (1) `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable — `statusText` may be empty for HTTP/2 or some responses. Use `!response.ok` or check `response.status`. (2) The entire new fetch block has no try/catch. If the network request fails (DNS error, connection refused, timeout), the rejection propagates unhandled from the constructor's promise chain, leaving `this.conn` in a rejected state and breaking all subsequent Salesforce operations with no clear error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED name is misleading

The constant is defined as `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, but the token refresh sync path additionally requires `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. Each call site that needs the sync path checks the constant AND the endpoint separately (e.g., in `refreshOAuthTokens.ts`), which is correct but error-prone. Consider either including the endpoint check in the constant or renaming it to reflect what it actually gates (e.g., `APP_CREDENTIAL_WEBHOOK_ENABLED`).

Encryption key length comment is wrong

The comment for `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` says "must be 32 bytes for AES256 encryption algorithm" and recommends `openssl rand -base64 24`. Base64-encoded 24 bytes decodes to 18 bytes, which is less than the 32 bytes (256 bits) required by AES-256. The correct command for 32 raw bytes is `openssl rand -base64 32` (which produces ~44 characters of base64). The `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` comment on line 91 has the same mistake but was not introduced by this PR.

No HTTP method check and no rate limiting

The handler processes any HTTP method (GET, PUT, DELETE, etc.) without checking `req.method`. It should explicitly accept only POST. Additionally, the endpoint has no rate limiting or brute-force protection beyond the shared secret. Combined with the non-constant-time comparison, an attacker who discovers the endpoint can attempt to brute-force the secret or flood it with requests.

No error handling around decryption and JSON parse

`symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` will throw if the key is missing, wrong, or the ciphertext is malformed. The subsequent `JSON.parse` will throw if the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON. Neither is wrapped in try/catch, so an invalid payload causes an unhandled exception and a 500 response, and the error details may leak. An attacker can probe the endpoint with random ciphertexts to enumerate behavior. Wrap in try/catch and return a 400 on decryption/parse failure.

No timeout on sync endpoint fetch

The `fetch` to the sync endpoint has no timeout. If the endpoint hangs or is slow, every token refresh in Cal.com will block on it, cascading into stalled calendar/video operations. Add an `AbortController` with a reasonable timeout (e.g., 10s).

Non-constant-time webhook secret comparison and header case bug

Two issues in the secret check: (1) `!==` on the header value is not constant-time, allowing timing side-channel attacks to recover the secret byte-by-byte. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. (2) `req.headers` keys are lowercased by Node, but the code looks up the header using `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` as-is. If a self-hoster sets the env to a mixed-case name, the lookup silently fails (the comparison becomes `undefined !== secret` which is always true), and the endpoint returns 403 for legitimate requests. Normalize the env var to lowercase before lookup, or always lowercase the key.

Outgoing request to sync endpoint has no authentication

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body. There is no shared secret, HMAC signature, or mutual TLS to authenticate the Cal.com instance to the self-hoster's endpoint. If the endpoint URL is discovered (e.g., via DNS enumeration or logs), an attacker can request refreshed tokens for arbitrary `calcomUserId` values, receiving valid access tokens for victims' third-party integrations. Add a signed payload (e.g., HMAC with a shared secret) or a bearer token header.

Race condition: no transaction around findFirst + create/update

The handler does `findFirst` then `create` or `update` in separate queries without a transaction. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appSlug)` can both find no existing credential, both attempt `create`, and either violate a unique constraint or produce duplicate credentials. The comment says "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential", but the solution is to wrap the findFirst+create in `prisma.$transaction`, or use a composite unique key on `(userId, appId)` and catch the unique violation to fall back to update.

Redirect URI hardcoded, inconsistent with callback.ts

The `add.ts` handler hardcodes `redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + "/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback"`, while the corresponding `callback.ts` (line 36) still uses `WEBAPP_URL + "/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback"`. If `appConfig.slug` is ever changed, the add and callback endpoints will use mismatched redirect URIs and OAuth will fail with a redirect_uri_mismatch error. Both files should use the same expression (preferably the config-based one).

Salesforce token refreshed on every service instantiation

The newly added block in `getClient` unconditionally fetches a new access token from Salesforce every time the method is called. Since `getClient` is invoked in the constructor (`this.conn = this.getClient(credential).then(c => c)`), every `new SalesforceCalendarService(credential)` — which happens for every booking/event involving Salesforce — triggers a token refresh request to Salesforce. This is a significant performance regression and risks hitting Salesforce API rate limits. The refresh should only happen when the existing token is expired or near expiry, matching the pattern used in other CalendarServices.

Sync path silently bypassed for team credentials without logging

The condition `... && userId` means that for team credentials (where `credential.userId` is null), the sync path is silently skipped and the normal refresh is used, even when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set. This means team-installed apps on self-hosted instances will continue refreshing against the self-hoster's OAuth client, not the parent's, which may be the intended behavior but is undocumented and surprising. At minimum, a log message should indicate that the sync path was skipped due to missing userId.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive while blacklist is lowercased

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased via `.toLowerCase()` on line 71, but the subsequent filter compares raw user input: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. A guest like `Bad@Example.com` is not matched against a blacklist entry `bad@example.com`, so any address whose case differs from the configured blacklist bypasses it entirely. Normalize the guest email (and ideally emails throughout the handler) to lowercase before comparing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner permission check uses && instead of ||

The `isTeamAdminOrOwner` flag is built with a logical AND of `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`, but the variable name and intent (`AdminOrOwner`) clearly indicates OR. As written, a team admin who is not also an owner fails the check (the only users who pass are owners, since being an owner typically implies being an admin). Any non-owner team admin (e.g. a delegated team manager) is silently denied permission even though the UI label and code path assume they can add guests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Email send uses raw input guests instead of filtered uniqueGuests

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the original input list rather than `uniqueGuests` (which excludes already-attending emails and blacklisted addresses). In `email-manager.ts` the recipient loop checks `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` to decide between sending a fresh `AttendeeScheduledEmail` vs. an `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. As a result, an existing attendee whose email is also present in the input gets a full "you're scheduled" confirmation email (with ICS file) instead of a "guests added" notification, and any email in the input that wasn't actually added is still considered "new" for routing. Pass `uniqueGuests` to `sendAddGuestsEmails` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Initial state seeds an empty string, so the first Add always fails validation

`useState<string[]>([""])` initializes the input with one empty email. The zod schema `z.array(z.string().email())` rejects empty strings, so clicking "Add" with the default state always shows the error banner before the user has even had a chance to type. Initialize with an empty array (matching `MultiEmail`'s empty-state branch) and add the empty input only after the user clicks "Add Emails".

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores disableStandardEmails settings

Every other send* function in this file honors `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` and `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail` (read from the event type metadata). `sendAddGuestsEmails` accepts no metadata and never checks these flags, so it always sends the organizer and attendee notifications regardless of how the event type is configured. Either thread the metadata through from the handler or look it up via the booking's eventType.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add arbitrary guests without organizer consent

Permission grants the addGuests capability not only to organizers and team admins/owners but also to any attendee (`isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)`). Combined with the lack of rate limiting, any invitee can enumerate or spam-add external email addresses to someone else's meeting. There is no confirmation from the organizer, and the organizer is only informed after the fact via `OrganizerAddGuestsEmail`. Either remove the attendee branch or require organizer approval.

Direct reassignment of a prop

`value = value || [];` mutates the `value` prop in place. While React does not re-render on prop mutation, this is misleading code and means subsequent reads use the mutated object reference. Use a default parameter (`value = []` in the signature) or a local `const emails = value ?? []`.

Email-send errors are swallowed with console.log

`catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` discards the error object entirely (notice `console.log` rather than `console.error`, and `err` is not used). Use `logger.error(...)` from `@calcom/lib/logger` like the rest of the file, and include `err` so the failure is diagnosable in production.

No check on booking status before mutating

The handler never inspects `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. It will happily persist new attendees onto CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-finished bookings, and `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` will then either fail or silently modify a calendar event for a meeting that no longer exists. The handler should reject mutations on non-ACCEPTED or past bookings.

No transaction / no error handling around calendar sync after DB update

`prisma.booking.update` writes the new attendees to the database first. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is then awaited with no try/catch. If the calendar integration throws (rate limit, expired token, network, etc.), the function rejects with a 500, but the database already has the new attendees persisted. Result: the Cal.com booking now lists guests that are NOT on the linked Google/Outlook calendar, and the user has no way to roll back. The whole flow should be wrapped in a transaction or, at minimum, the calendar sync should happen first so a failure leaves the system consistent.

Using array index as React key in the email list

`value.map((field, index) => <li key={index} ...)` reuses keys when emails are added/removed, which causes React to reuse input components and can lose focus/caret position or render stale values for the newly inserted empty input. Use a stable id (e.g. include the email value or a counter ref).

addGuests uses authedProcedure instead of bookingsProcedure

Sibling mutations that touch a booking (`editLocation`, `confirm`, etc.) use `bookingsProcedure`, which typically enforces booking-level permission middleware. `addGuests` is wired with the looser `authedProcedure`, so any authenticated user can hit the endpoint and the only authorization is the handler's own checks (which have the bugs noted above). Use `bookingsProcedure` for consistency and to inherit the centralized guards.

attendees[0].name accessed without null check in email subject

The subject template reads `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. If `attendees` is empty this throws a TypeError that aborts the email; if `attendees[0].name` is null/undefined the subject renders as "Guests Added: <eventType> with  at <date>". Add a guard or fall back to the organizer/team name.

isInvalidEmail flag is not cleared after a successful mutation

On validation failure `setIsInvalidEmail(true)` is called, but neither `onSuccess` nor `handleAdd` ever resets it back to false. A user who first submits invalid emails, then fixes them and successfully adds guests, will continue to see the red "Emails must be unique and valid" banner in the dialog (and after reopening the dialog for the same booking) until the Cancel button is clicked. Reset the flag at the start of `handleAdd` and inside `onSuccess`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount update uses stale in-memory value (lost-update race)

Both the `else` branch (line 179) and the `catch` block (line 190) write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, where `reminder.retryCount` is the value returned by the `findMany` at the top of the handler. If two cron invocations overlap, or the same reminder is picked up twice within one run, both workers read the same starting value and both write `start + 1`, so the counter only advances by one instead of two. That means under overlap a reminder can take 3–4 actual attempts to reach `retryCount > 1` and be deleted, breaking the "after two failures" guarantee stated in the PR description. The update should be a relative increment (e.g. `{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`) so concurrent workers compose correctly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount-based deletion is method-agnostic

The new `deleteMany` clause `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` is placed in the top-level `OR` without any `method` filter, so it will delete EMAIL and WHATSAPP `WorkflowReminder` rows in addition to SMS ones. The rest of the handler only processes SMS (the `findMany` is restricted to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`), and only the SMS path increments `retryCount`, so today this is latent — but the schema field is shared and the next contributor who increments `retryCount` for, say, WhatsApp will silently start dropping those rows here. The retry-clause should be scoped to SMS (e.g. `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 }`) so the deletion rule matches the rule that produces the counter.

false_positives.candidate:
Error log drops reminder context

The catch block only logs `Error scheduling SMS with error ${error}`. It does not include the `reminder.id`, `bookingUid`, `workflowStepId`, or the `sendTo`/recipient, so when the new retry path deletes a reminder after two failures there is no trail in logs tying the deletion back to a specific booking or recipient. For a feature whose entire purpose is to stop silently retrying bad recipients, the error log should at minimum include the reminder id and recipient so on-call can correlate the eventual deletion with the original failure.

No tests cover the new retry/delete behavior

The PR adds a new column, changes the deletion predicate, and introduces two new update sites, but ships no tests for the new behavior. Specifically there is no test covering: (a) `retryCount` increments on `twilio.scheduleSMS` returning a falsy value, (b) `retryCount` increments in the catch block, (c) reminders with `retryCount > 1` are deleted by the next run, (d) reminders with `retryCount <= 1` are not deleted. Without these, a future refactor of the OR/deleteMany/findMany queries could regress the cap without being caught.

Retry-based deletion ignores `scheduled` and may drop already-scheduled reminders

The `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` branch in the top-level `OR` of the `deleteMany` runs without checking `scheduled` or `referenceId`. Today only the failure path increments `retryCount`, so this is latent — but if any future change ever bumps `retryCount` after a successful schedule (for example as part of a send-status callback, or by an SMS_RECEIVED/RECEIPT webhook reconciliation that double-writes), reminders that were already handed off to Twilio will be deleted here while the provider still has a live scheduled message, producing a phantom-delivery bug with no audit row. AssignmentSource.queued default evaluated once at class definition time

The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a well-known Python dataclass pitfall: `timezone.now()` is called once when the class body executes (at module import), not each time an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every instance created without an explicit `queued` will share the same import-time timestamp, so `queued` no longer represents "when this assignment source was queued". Fix by importing `field` from `dataclasses` and writing `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The current test only asserts `queued is not None`, which masks the bug. The field is not yet consumed by any logic, but it is part of the persisted payload and any future use for TTL, deduplication, or staleness checks will be wrong.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead method _create_process_for_shard

The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase. The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` always uses `_create_process_for_shards` to bring back the whole process (and therefore all shards mapped to it). Either delete the dead method, or use it as a true per-shard restart hook so that one bad shard doesn't take down its siblings sharing the same process.

Dead-branch check `if not process`

Inside `_ensure_processes_alive` the loop guards with `if not process: continue`. `self.processes` is a `dict[int, SpawnProcess | Thread]` and is only ever assigned live objects in `_create_process_for_shards`, so this guard can never be true and serves no purpose. The subsequent `if not process.is_alive():` already covers dead processes, so this line should be removed to avoid misleading readers.

Distribution test does not verify per-process assignment

The test `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts only that the total number of shards assigned across all processes equals 4 (`total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()) == 4`). This passes even if the modulo distribution is broken — for example, all four shards could be assigned to a single process, or a shard could be duplicated across processes — as long as the total counts to 4. The test never submits spans, so it does not exercise the actual per-process flushing of shared shards either. There should be explicit assertions like `assert flusher.process_to_shards_map == {0: [0, 2], 1: [1, 3]}` and a round-trip test that submits spans on each partition and verifies they get flushed.

Off-by-one in MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS allows one extra restart

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the check `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` happens *before* `self.process_restarts[process_index] += 1`. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10`, the sequence is 0,1,...,10 (pass), 11 (fail). That means the consumer tolerates 11 restarts of a given process before giving up, not 10 as the constant name suggests. Either increment before the check or use `>=` so the documented limit matches behavior.

max_processes=0 silently becomes 'one process per shard'

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats `0` the same as `None` because `0 or X` evaluates to `X`. A caller that explicitly passes `0` (e.g., a test, or a future config switch) gets the opposite of what they asked for. Use `if max_processes is not None else len(...)` so `0` is honored as "no flusher processes".

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Assert failure leaves partition stuck forever

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the assert `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is performed before accessing `message.value`. If it fails (or any other error occurs before we can safely read `message.value`), the `except Exception` handler re-checks `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` — which is the same condition that just failed — and silently does nothing. The offset for that message is never added to the tracker, so it stays outstanding and blocks every future commit for that partition in `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` (which iterates only up to the highest completed offset). The consumer will hang on this partition indefinitely, with only a log line as evidence. The error should either be re-raised so arroyo/DLQ can handle it, or the offset must be marked complete unconditionally (even if `BrokerValue` can't be read) by carrying the partition/offset before the assert.

Docstring claims natural backpressure but queue is unbounded

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. However, the queues are constructed via `queue.Queue()` (see `FixedQueuePool.__init__`), which is unbounded. Producers (the arroyo consumer thread calling `submit`) will never block, so a slow worker group causes unbounded memory growth. Either pass `maxsize` to `queue.Queue(maxsize=...)` to actually provide backpressure, or correct the docstring.

Graceful shutdown drops in-flight queue items

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` checks `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `self.work_queue.get()`, workers exit the loop as soon as the flag is observed and never drain items that were already in their queue. Those items have offsets recorded as outstanding in `OffsetTracker`, but since `complete_offset` is never called, they will never be committed and the messages will be re-delivered after restart. The `wait_until_empty` helper exists on the same class but is never invoked, indicating the intent was to drain but the implementation doesn't. Either remove the `wait_until_empty` helper or call it (with a bounded timeout) before flipping the shutdown flag.

Hash-based group assignment is not stable across restarts

`FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses Python's built-in `hash()`, which is randomized per process under the default `PYTHONHASHSEED`. The class docstring promises 'consistent hashing' and 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue'. Within a single process lifetime the assignment is stable (since workers/queues live in memory), but after any restart the same `group_key` can map to a different queue index — directly contradicting the docstring. This is misleading to future maintainers and would break correctness if the pool is ever extended to persist queue assignments or run across processes. Use a stable hash (e.g. `hashlib.sha1(group_key.encode()).hexdigest()`, `zlib.crc32`, or `hashlib.md5`) and update the docstring to reflect the actual guarantee.

Integration test relies on arroyo private internals

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. The leading underscore marks these as private arroyo APIs; their names/signatures are not part of arroyo's public contract and can change without warning, breaking this test (and the CI signal it provides) on an arroyo upgrade. Use the public `StreamProcessor.run()` method (which blocks until the consumer stops) instead, with a bounded stop condition or shutdown timeout, so the test exercises the same path real deployments use.

Kafka integration test only waits 5 seconds for 5 messages

In `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit`, the test produces 5 messages and then runs `processor._run_once()` in a loop for only 5 seconds. The assertions then require that `commit_count >= 1` and that the committed offset reached 5, but the producer flush + consumer rebalance + first poll can easily eat most of that budget on a loaded CI box, producing a flaky test. Wait for `stats["total_items"] == 0` (as the other tests in this file do) before tearing the processor down, and assert on the committed offset only after that condition is met.

Offset tracker scans full range per partition every second

`OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` is called once per second from `_commit_loop` and, for each partition, computes `min(all_offsets)` and `max(all_offsets)` and then iterates the full range `range(start, max_offset + 1)`. With a partition that has, say, 10k outstanding offsets, every commit tick performs O(10k) set lookups plus two O(n) set scans. For a backlog scenario this is O(n) per second per partition. Track `min_offset` and `max_offset` incrementally (e.g. on `add_offset`) and stop as soon as the first gap is hit instead of recomputing the extremes every call.

Worker shutdown flag is a non-atomic bool

`OrderedQueueWorker.shutdown` is a plain `bool` attribute written by the main thread (in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`) and read by the worker thread. While CPython's GIL makes this safe in practice, it is not portable and is not thread-safe by Python's memory model. Use `threading.Event` (`self._stop_event`) and `self._stop_event.is_set()` instead, matching the pattern already used by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.shutdown_event`.

Worker thread can die silently on unexpected get() error

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` only catches `queue.ShutDown` around `self.work_queue.get()`. Any other exception raised by `get()` (e.g. an OS-level error, a future Python version change) propagates out of `run()` and kills the daemon thread silently — items remaining in that queue will never be processed and their offsets will never be marked complete, permanently blocking that partition's commits. Wrap the call in a broader `except Exception` that logs and either retries or exits cleanly, and consider asserting the worker is still alive from a supervisor.

max_workers silently coerced to 20 when zero/falsy

`num_queues=max_workers or 20` falls back to 20 whenever `max_workers` is `None`, `0`, or any other falsy value. An operator who passes `--max-workers 0` to disable the new mode will instead get 20 queues/workers started, with no log or error. The fallback should be explicit (`max_workers if max_workers else 20` is functionally the same but at minimum document the behavior, or raise on non-positive values so operators notice the misconfiguration).

num_queues is not validated

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` accepts `num_queues: int = 20` without checking it is positive. If a caller (or the new `thread-queue-parallel` mode) passes `max_workers=0` or a negative value, the loop creates no queues/workers, and the first call to `submit` raises `IndexError` from `self.queues[queue_index]` deep in `FixedQueuePool.submit`. Validate `num_queues >= 1` (and ideally a sensible upper bound) at construction time so misconfiguration fails loudly and early.

The test still passes because the denial cache is hit first, but the comment misrepresents what the permCache entry contains and could mislead anyone reading it. false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
List does not fall back to DB when the permCache is stale, leaving newly created items invisible

In the new List() the only DB fallback is on a complete cache miss (getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cache.ErrNotFound). If the user already has a populated permCache for the action, List trusts it as-is and never requeries. Compare with Check() (lines 123-136) which now requeries when the cached scopeMap does not contain the requested name/folder. The PR's stated goal — 'dash/folder creator can't access the dashboard/folder that they've just created' — is therefore only fixed for Check; a user who navigates to the dashboards list immediately after creating a dashboard will not see the new entry until the permCache expires (30s). Either List should also requery when the requested name/folder is absent from the cached scopes, or at minimum the dashboard/folder create path should invalidate or refresh the relevant permCache entries.

PermDenialCache can block legitimate access after permission grant or resource recreation

The permDenialCache is consulted at the very start of Check() (lines 116-121) and short-circuits to Allowed:false without ever touching the DB or the permCache. The denial is written at lines 153-155 whenever checkPermission returns false, with a 30-second TTL (shortCacheTTL). Because the denial entry is never invalidated when permissions change or resources are created, the following scenarios keep a freshly-authorised user locked out for up to 30 seconds: (1) user A previously failed a check on resource X (e.g. before X existed or before the grant), the entry is cached, then X is created with A as owner / A is added to a team that grants access — the next Check still hits the denial key and denies; (2) the same happens when a resource is deleted and later recreated with the same UID under new ownership; (3) a race where A asks for X before the create-grant transaction commits — A is denied, the denial is cached, and once the transaction commits A still cannot access X until the entry expires. This re-introduces precisely the 'creator cannot access the dashboard/folder they just created' symptom this PR is supposed to fix. Consider only caching denials for resources known to exist, invalidating the entry on permission change, or dropping the TTL drastically.

false_positives.candidate:
Creating and Deleting transient states no longer rendered

The previous version fetched both Prometheus and Ruler groups and used `matchRules` to distinguish three cases: rules present in both (normal), rules only in ruler (rendered with `RuleOperation.Creating`), and rules only in Prometheus (rendered with `RuleOperation.Deleting`). This PR removes the Ruler fetch and the entire matching logic, so rules that are in the middle of being created/deleted will silently appear as ordinary active rules, with no Creating/Deleting badge. The `operation={RuleOperation.Creating}` and `RuleOperationListItem` props are still accepted by `GrafanaRuleListItem` but nothing ever computes them now.

Delete menu item never renders in the list view

The Delete menu is gated by `canDelete && rulerRule && (...)`. In the list view the consumer (`GrafanaRuleListItem`/`RuleActionsButtons.V2`) only passes `promRule`, so `rulerRule` is `undefined`. The new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` evaluates `canDelete` to `true` for users with delete permission on Grafana folders, but the render guard short-circuits to `false` and the Delete option is hidden anyway. Effectively users will not be able to delete Grafana-managed rules from the list view even though the abilities hook reports they can.

Pause menu item never renders in the list view

The Pause menu item is gated by `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'`. In the list view `rulerRule` is `undefined`, so `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(undefined)` returns `false` and the Pause option is hidden even though `canPause` (computed via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`) may be true. Users lose the ability to pause Grafana-managed rules from the list view.

Redundant triple mock reset in beforeEach

The `beforeEach` block calls `jest.clearAllMocks(); jest.restoreAllMocks(); jest.resetAllMocks();` sequentially. Calling all three is redundant (each fully resets call/spy state) and can mask the intent of which reset is actually needed. Pick the single appropriate call. Also, because the mocks are then re-set up immediately with default returns, the order/selection matters: if `clearAllMocks` is removed, the previously installed `mockImplementation` from the previous test would persist for unwired mocks, potentially producing subtle cross-test contamination.

Stale `// duplicate` comment in useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities

Line 289 in `useAbilities.ts` reads: `const { isEditable, isRemovable, loading } = useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(rule); // duplicate`. The trailing `// duplicate` looks like a leftover TODO/scratchpad marker. It is meaningless to future readers and should be removed or replaced with an explanatory comment.

Tests for Creating/Deleting transient state were deleted

The original `GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx` covered `should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists` and `should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists`, plus three unit tests for `matchRules`. All have been removed in this PR. Since the deletion of those behaviors is a regression risk (see the previous finding), these tests should be retained (or replaced with new tests asserting the new equivalent behavior) to prevent re-introducing the bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Brittle call-count assertion masks the duplicate-interpolation waste

The test pins expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5), which depends on the exact number of shard groups produced by the specific fetchLabelValues fixture plus the 1+N pattern above. Any change to grouping size, fetchLabelValues results, or the runSplitQuery call sites will break this test even when the user-visible behavior is correct. The assertion exists only to document the redundant call from runShardSplitQuery through runSplitQuery; it should instead verify the intended contract (e.g. that queries are interpolated exactly once before the first runQuery call) so a regression that introduces or removes duplicate interpolation is caught.

Queries are interpolated twice in the shard-splitting flow

runShardSplitQuery now interpolates each query (line 49-52), then passes the already-interpolated targets into splitQueriesByStreamShard. For every shard group, runNextRequest (line 163) calls runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...) with that subRequest, and the new runSplitQuery in querySplitting.ts (line 296-299) re-applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to the same queries. The result is 1 + N interpolations of the same queries (N = number of shard groups). The test on line 112 of shardQuerySplitting.test.ts even pins this in place with expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5). It works only because the template-service replacement is idempotent on the substituted values, but it is wasted work on every shard group iteration, and any future interpolation that is not strictly idempotent (e.g. counters, suffixes, timestamps) will silently produce wrong results or repeated side effects on the same query objects.
